title: Judge issues $75K warning after labour hire firm fails to pay foreign workers
text:
A federal judge says a $75,600 fine for a labour hire company should put any other organisations that might be failing to pay their workers properly on notice.

Four Seasons Workforce and its director Pik Yok Chey were fined in the Federal Court after the firm was found to have failed to comply with two notices issued by the Fair Work Ombudsman.

The compliance notices required the company to back-pay entitlements to two migrant workers who it had supplied to pick blueberries on Coffs Harbour region farms.

In his judgment, Judge Robert Cameron said the workers were vulnerable given they were employed as pieceworkers on temporary visas and had limited English skills.

"A penalty should be of a kind that would deter similar contraventions by like-minded persons or organisations," he wrote.

"A failure to comply with a statutory notice is serious."

The workers had worked on blueberry farms. (ABC Rural: Brandon Long)

The Fair Work Ombudsman became aware of Four Seasons Workforce underpaying workers after it received two complaints from Chinese and Japanese backpackers.

The pair worked for the company at different intervals in 2023 and 2024.

The company was fined $63,000, while Ms Chey was fined $12,600 as Four Seasons Workforce's sole director.

The Fair Work Ombudsman said the workers were paid on a piecework basis according to the total weight of the blueberries they picked.

The ombudsman's media director Matthew Raggatt said the labour hire firm failed to pay them the guaranteed minimum rate, which was applied across the horticulture award.

"So for each day you work as a pieceworker, you have to be paid no less than the minimum hourly rate for casual fruit pickers under the relevant award," he said.

Kun Du worked on a blueberry farm in the Coffs Harbour region. (Supplied)

Chinese National Kun Du, who was one of the two workers involved in the case, said in a statement earlier this year that others should not be afraid to come forward.

"I just want to tell them to be brave, to fight for yourself and fight for more people," she said at the time.

" If you need help, you can access people's help. Don't be afraid. Be brave. "

More investigations underway

Mr Raggatt said the case against Ms Chey and Four Seasons Workforce was not the only case it had taken to court this year, as it continued investigations into the horticulture sector across the Coffs Coast and Nambucca Valley.

"Those investigations are ongoing, but we have filed another litigation [against an individual] in 2026 in the Coffs Harbour region, and that was in July," he said.

He said that case involved the alleged underpayment of two Japanese fruit pickers working on a farm in Halfway Creek, north of Coffs Harbour.

Matthew Raggatt says pieceworkers need to be paid the minimum hourly rate according to the award. (Supplied: Matthew Raggatt)

It has been alleged the two workers were underpaid about $7,000 over a seven-week period. The matter is still before the courts.

Elsewhere, the ombudsman secured more than $180,000 in penalties in Queensland in August this year in a case involving the horticulture industry.

Mr Raggatt said compliance notices were issued before court action was taken to give employers a chance to rectify the issue.

He said improving compliance in this sector and taking action to protect migrant workers were priorities for the regulator.

"Where employers do not comply, including with compliance notices, we will take appropriate action to protect employees," he said.

title: John Setka expelled by CFMEU, denies 'misappropriating' $3.3m in union funds
text:
Former Victorian CFMEU boss John Setka says an allegation from the union's administration that he misappropriated more than $3 million in member funds is "absolute bullshit" and he plans to appeal his expulsion.

In a statement his afternoon, the CFMEU's administration said it had expelled Mr Setka from the organisation after he had faced 27 disciplinary charges under union rules.

"An investigation by the CFMEU administration alleged Setka had failed in his duty as secretary of the union and diverted $3.3 million in revenue from union merchandise and site vending machines to his companies," union administrators said in a statement.

In the statement, CFMEU administrator Michael Crosby said the union would pursue Mr Setka in a bid to recover "the millions that his company has received".

The CFMEU administration says John Setka's expulsion will take effect immediately and last five years. (AAP: Joel Carrett)

"John Setka held a position of responsibility but abused that privilege to take millions of dollars from the members of the CFMEU," Mr Crosby alleged.

"John Setka's conduct is shameful. He has failed in the most basic duties of a union official — to put members' interests above all."

The union administration said Mr Setka did not respond to them about the allegations.

John Setka says allegations are 'absolute lies'

The press release did not provide specifics of the alleged misappropriation and the ABC does not suggest the claims are true.

When contacted by the ABC, Mr Setka said the allegation was "absolute bullshit".

"I will be going to court, and I will be appealing the decision because its absolute lies and it's defamatory," he said.

"I have never taken one dollar of union members' money — that is an absolute lie."

Mr Setka led the Victorian division of the CFMEU for several years. (AAP: Stefan Postles)

The CFMEU administration said Mr Setka's expulsion would take effect immediately and last for a "legal maximum term of five years".

The construction arm of the CFMEU has been in administration since 2024, amid allegations of corruption and bullying in the union.

In September, Mr Setka faced court over an Instagram post he allegedly made attacking union administration figures.

title: Tribute to former Adelaide Hills passenger rail in backyard model
text:
Calls may be continuing for a reinstated passenger railway service to the Adelaide Hills, but a world away from public transport lobbying, Peter Michalak is building his own version in a backyard shed.

Harking back to the late 1980s and early 90s, Mr Michalak's HO scale (1:87) Hills Line railway layout represents the 315-kilometre stretch between Adelaide and Serviceton, just over the Victorian border.

Featuring the Murray Mallee town of Pinnaroo and Tailem Bend railway station with buildings modelled to scale, its centrepiece is Bridgewater railway station in the Adelaide Hills, complete with the old mill and tree-covered hillside.

Peter Michalak's layout includes the historic Bridgewater Mill in the Adelaide Hills. (891 ABC Adelaide: Malcolm Sutton)

"Bridgewater, in this reality, still has passenger train services to it," Mr Michalak said.

"I grew up catching SteamRanger [heritage] trains to Bridgewater as a kid in the school holidays, so I had a lot of memories of going up there, and I had to create it."

Bridgewater was the first railway station he created, and was designed to be portable and taken on exhibit.

The railway line goes through Pinnaroo, a town in SA's Murray Mallee. (891 ABC Adelaide: Malcolm Sutton)

The layout, which Mr Michalak started in 2013, has since grown too big and too complicated to be exhibited.

It now gives a "selectively compressed" version of the much longer railway, and includes Mount Lofty Railway Station, while his brother, Nick, is currently building Blackwood Railway Station.

Peter Michalak has been working on his Hills Line HO scale since 2013. (891 ABC Adelaide: Malcolm Sutton)

Mr Michalak has built about 50 metres of mainline rail, which loops around his shed over three levels, and hosts some very familiar trains built to scale.

"The only difference being, instead of running a 70-wagon container train, I'm running a 10-wagon container train because you obviously don't have the real estate to play with," Mr Michalak said.

"The platforms are also shortened, along with some other bits and pieces that have been selectively compressed to fit the space we've got."

An intricate model of Tailem Bend Railway Station in the Murray Mallee. (891 ABC Adelaide: Malcolm Sutton)

A freight train engine even makes realistic sounds as it trundles past Bridgewater, with trees fashioned from the sedum "autumn joy" plant.

The engine whines through the hills and at one point lets loose a blast from its horn that could have come from the gullies of Belair.

A tunnel along the Adelaide Hills railway line replicated by Peter Michalak's model. (891 ABC Adelaide: Malcolm Sutton)

Mr Michalak is focused on building part of the once sprawling Adelaide Railway Station at the end of the line, which is being modelled on its appearance before the convention centre was built over part of the station in 1987.

His layout even includes the "international orange chairs" on the platform.

The model even includes the orange seating on the station platform. (Facebook: The Hills Line in HO scale)

He said his model of Serviceton Railway Station, with its heritage-listed two-storey brick complex, when finished "will probably be the key piece".

"Particularly given the size of the building that has to be built for that, it's going to be the real showpiece for the whole layout, but that's still a long way down the track," Mr Michalak said.

"It has a cardboard mock-up stuck to the back wall at the moment."

Not quite finished, the model station currently has a cardboard exterior background. (891 ABC Adelaide: Malcolm Sutton)

The layout also includes a different branch line to Port Adelaide where a mill, based on the heritage Hart's Mill building, is modelled.

Mr Michalak estimates it will be another 10 years until the project is fully completed.

The scene includes a model of the Hart's Mill building in Port Adelaide. (891 ABC Adelaide: Malcolm Sutton)

Nick Michalak undertakes the computer-aided design drawings (CAD) and Mr Michalak 3D-prints the train engine and carriage components.

Some trains can be sourced, such as freight trains with a national profile, but many of those unique to South Australia have to be constructed by hand.

A model engine that had to be made for his collection. (891 ABC Adelaide: Malcolm Sutton)

This includes the classic SA-built Redhen passenger series, which was in service across the metropolitan area from the 1950s to 1996.

They even took passengers into the Adelaide Hills, a service that was progressively wound back by the state government in the 1980s before it stopped altogether at Belair in 1987.

Far from reality

There has been growing pressure on the government to reinstate passenger rail transport to the hills due to its increasing population and rising congestion on the South Eastern Freeway.

SA voters' transport wishlist As more houses are being built in Adelaide's outer suburbs, more public transport is something on the minds of South Australian voters, in both the regions and the city.

Mr Michalak, who is also the SteamRanger Heritage Railway vice-president, would love to see it reinstated into the hills from Adelaide.

"Unfortunately, I think we've got a better chance of aliens being located and wanting to come and talk to us than getting our state government to commit to doing rail in the hills," he said.

"It's a shame because it's not that hard. It's just there's a lack of willpower to do it."

Peter Michalak with a passenger train his brother made for the set. (891 ABC Adelaide: Malcolm Sutton)

Helping to run a number of real-life steam- and diesel-hauled passenger trains between Mount Barker and Victor Harbor for tourists, Mr Michalak continues to work on his own layout at home, finding the occasional hour or two in the shed between full-time work, volunteering and family life.

Taking the creation as seriously as any number of similar enthusiasts across the city, Mr Michalak's friend, a former South Australian Railways and national train controller, has even drawn up train control graphs that replicate the real railway's timetable.

Bridgewater was the first setting Peter Michalak created and has been exhibited. (891 ABC Adelaide: Malcolm Sutton)

The timetable, however, will compress a 12-hour shift into about a two-and-a-half-hour window.

"The idea is that we crack a few beers and we have someone here controlling the train movements," Mr Michalak said.

"It's a very social part of it all.

"It's built to use."

title: How a small scrap of sandpaper shed light on cricket's so-called dark arts
text:
Eight years after then-prime minister Malcolm Turnbull felt the need to weigh in on Australia's ball tampering in the Cape Town Test, sandpaper and cricket are back in the headlines together.

Usman Khawaja's book, featuring revelations, allusions and confirmations of what most everyone already believed, has reignited conversations about the Australian team's conduct during that 2018 tour of South Africa.

But whatever the team did, who did it and who knew about it, one thing is for sure: they weren't the first to fiddle with the ball.

So why did they do it and why was the reaction so extreme?

'A beautiful art'

Reverse swing can make even the best batters look silly. (Getty Images: Tom Shaw)

In the wake of Khawaja's exclusive interview with Nine Newspapers on the weekend, outspoken former Australia fast bowler Geoff Lawson added to the conversation with a brilliantly headlined article.

" I don't know a bowler who hasn't licked, flicked, scratched or slobbered on a cricket ball. "

Thanks for those mental images, Geoff.

Evocative wording or not, the 46-Test veteran is right. But why?

Explaining the mysteries of swing bowling It is one of the most devastating weapons a fast bowler can own — but the art of swing is steeped in mystery and myths that only science can explain.

The science of conventionally swinging a cricket ball through the air is relatively simple and adheres to some basic rules of drag, air pressure and laminar flow (a lot of the same stuff that keeps an aeroplane in the air).

When a cricket ball is new, its stitched seam is standing at its tallest, allowing a bowler to angle that seam towards or away from the batter and the air will get caught on the seam, dragging the ball in that direction.

But the proud seam on a dark red ball is clearly visible to a batter, and the best ones can see what's happening and account for it.

Reverse swing is a little more complicated and prized due to it being more difficult to deliver, predict and face.

Conventional swing (left) vs reverse swing (right). (ABC News: Gabrielle Flood and Nina Maile Gordon)

"As a batter it's the hardest thing to face. It's a beautiful art," former Proteas captain Faf du Plessis told The Grade Cricketer podcast on the eve of Australia's return to Cape Town last month.

The ball swings towards the side of the ball that looks smoother due to small abrasions on that "shiny" side of the ball, more of which is facing the batter and therefore offering more surface area and turbulent airflow, this time dragging the ball in the opposite direction to the way the seam is facing.

It also happens later in the ball's flight, often too late for the batter to react.

It only comes after the ball has been bowled for a few dozen overs and whacked around the field a bit; once the seam has flattened out, and the leather has been, crucially, roughed up and dried out.

Weather conditions have to be perfect, the bowlers have to be incredibly skilled and the care for the ball has to be spot-on, to the point that former England captain Alastair Cook was prized as a ball shiner because he barely sweats.

Of course, there are other ways to help this along.

Spit, sunscreen and swing

There are plenty of legal ways to shine the ball. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

Once a cricket pitch has flattened out from the start of a game, the new ball has lost its shine and proud seam, and before it becomes a spinner's paradise on days four and five (although this is becoming more and more rare), reverse swing is one of the few tools in fast bowler's arsenal.

For decades, cricket teams have worked on the ball feverishly to try to work on conventional and reverse swing.

Often players will shine the ball on their groin or hip, or some sweat from their forehead (or spit in pre-COVID times).

In those processes, there are some grey areas.

Any sensible cricketer will be wearing sunscreen, some will be wearing hair products, many will be chewing gum or chomping on a lolly.

Sweat can be used to shine the ball but keeping it dry is key to reverse swing. (Getty Images: Stu Forster)

All of that gives a little extra viscosity to the sweat or saliva used on the ball, but match referees couldn't very well force players to spit their gum into a hanky on the boundary line or force them to have a shower before entering the field of play, so there is not much they can do.

Then there's the flip side, where players try to create a rougher surface to generate that turbulent airflow, which can include simple things like picking at the seam of a ball or fielders intentionally throwing the ball in short to ensure it bounces on the coarse pitch block.

Ironically enough, du Plessis, South Africa's captain on that fateful 2018 tour, twice stumbled from lightish grey into gun-metal territory earlier in his career.

In 2013, after a failed attempt with his fingernails, du Plessis was caught on camera blatantly scratching the ball on the zip of his pants pocket, mere centimetres from legal territory.

Teams work hard on the ball to create the conditions for conventional and reverse swing bowling. (Getty Images: Santanu Banik/MB Media)

A few years later, as he skippered the team during a 2016 tour of Australia, he was again seen on the field opening his mouth, touching his fingers to a massive white mint on the middle of his tongue, then applying that sugary saliva directly to the ball.

Had he simply sucked the mint, popped it into his cheek and then touched his tongue, he could have avoided his own chase through the airport and a hefty fine.

Du Plessis described the fallout from his 2013 zipper incident as "a week of hell", so it's no wonder he expressed so much sympathy for Cameron Bancroft and Steve Smith (curiously no mention of David Warner) as the world closed in on them.

After massive bans and public disgrace, you would think the world would have moved on, but between the long-awaited Test return to South Africa and now Khawaja's book, the controversy seems never-ending.

Why the sandpaper saga?

One part absolutely boils to down to Australian cricket's sense of exceptionalism and perception of itself as arbiter of what is and isn't acceptable on a cricket field.

But the brazen nature of the ball tampering is perhaps the biggest reason that this was and remains such a big story.

Sandpapergate continues to wound Australia Usman Khawaja and David Warner's Sandpapergate revelations may have set the scene for civil war in Australian cricket as the 2018 ball-tampering scandal continues to captivate and damage.

England skipper Michael Atherton was caught rubbing dirt into the ball and his reputation remains pristine but, like the various fructose or lotion-enhanced bodily fluids, that's the sort of thing one could use on the ball opportunistically or even inadvertently.

Perhaps that's why Bancroft's first feeble attempt at deflection was claiming he "saw an opportunity to potentially use some tape [and] get some granules from the rough patches on the wicket", rather than bringing some 300 grit onto the field where its only purpose could be ball tampering.

There are legendary tales of bottle caps being used to help out reverse swing kings like Wasim Akram and Waqar Younis in Test matches way back when, and Khawaja wrote about some of the methods he had seen or heard of in Sheffield Shield cricket.

But in a high-profile Test series, to be so obvious when the team knew they already had heat on them betrayed a sense that they thought they were untouchable or that winning was worth the risk.

Alas, the SuperSport cameras caught him in high definition and super slow-mo and put the so-called dark arts very much under a spotlight.

After du Plessis's minty moment, Dirk Nannes said in commentary at the time for ABC Sport: "It's an art and some of the art is doing it and not getting caught."

If that is the case, consider Cameron Bancroft less Gauguin and more Gallagher.

title: ACL battles haven't halted these AFL draft hopefuls
text:
In just the second game of this year's footy season, Gus White did not realise he had suffered an ACL injury when he hurt his knee.

"I landed a bit funny and hyperextended my knee … it didn't hurt that bad," he said.

" I went and got scans a couple of days later, the result came back with the ACL, which was really devastating. "

The 18-year-old is one of many teenage footballers vying for a chance in the AFL draft later this month — and is hopeful he will be in contention, despite only playing one full game of football this year.

"I'm obviously really nervous, not having much control over my playing this year," he said.

For months, White has been firmly focused on recovery. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

White said he initially sat in the emotions of the injury but quickly shifted his focus.

"I just gave myself 24 to 48 hours to sit in my thoughts and really feel it and from then move on and accept that it's happened," he said.

" 'Control the controllables' was the main goal — and [to] just stay as positive as I could. "

The South Adelaide product just hit the six-month milestone of recovery, a significant halfway mark of an injury that sidelines most players for about a year.

'Every journey's different'

When the injury first happened, White spoke to someone who had trodden the same path a year earlier.

North Adelaide's Memphis Webb injured his ACL last year. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

It was round 2 of the 2025 SANFL season when North Adelaide's Memphis Webb injured his ACL.

"The 12 months was long, but I made strategies and figured out ways to get through it," he said.

Webb decided to step away from football for the year as he recovered.

"I learnt a lot about myself, because before that my life had pretty much just been football," he said.

" Obviously it wasn't great not playing footy for a year, but it was almost a blessing as well. "

Webb stepped away from football for a year. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

The 18-year-old said the recovery process had given him a lot of time to reflect, and had reignited his love for football when finally returned to playing in round 4 this year.

"I was like a little kid again, playing footy for the first time," Webb said.

The midfielder said he was at the match, but not yet back playing, when White did his ACL against North Adelaide in round 2.

"We had a good chat about things to expect for him — I just said, 'Every journey's different, don't try and compare to other people'," he said.

Webb returned to the field earlier this year. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

White said Webb was one of the first people he went to about his injury.

"I asked him how he dealt with things and what worked for him, what didn't," White said.

White, who is also a midfielder, said seeing someone else experience the same injury and return to the field after such a hard time was motivating.

"It sort of opens that light at the end of the tunnel," he said.

White says discussion with Webb helped boost confidence in recovery. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

'Dream to play AFL footy'

White was invited to the AFL Draft Combine, where top junior prospects undergo physical testing and interviews, but was unable to be involved.

He was hopeful his junior years of footy had been enough to show prospective AFL clubs what he could achieve.

"Ever since I was four years old, it's been the dream to play AFL footy, so if my name were to be called out on draft night, I'll be over the moon," he said.

Webb is prepared for all eventualities. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

Webb was also invited to the national combine but instead featured at the state event due to sickness.

While feeling nervous ahead of the draft, he was grateful for the experience so far.

"Not many people my age get to experience this journey that I've been on," he said.

" I'm just looking forward to it, whatever happens will happen. "

The AFL draft will be held over two nights on November 19 and 20.

title: Aussie filmmakers left scrambling amid David Walliams allegations
text:
The Australian producers of Fing!, an upcoming children's movie based on a book by David Walliams, have confirmed his cameo has been removed from the film following allegations against the comedian.

Its distributor, Transmission Films, has also confirmed that Walliams, a co-writer on the movie, will also be removed from its publicity, and its streaming distributor Stan has confirmed it will no longer release the movie.

In an investigation published by The Guardian and ITV, Walliams is alleged to have groomed teenage fans and sexually assaulted a 15-year-old girl, and to have harassed young female colleagues.

Walliams, who lost a High Court battle to avoid being identified in the UK media and did not appeal the decision, denied targeting teenagers and using his fame to manipulate them to have sex, his lawyers said.

A UK/Australia co-production, Fing! stars Taika Waititi, Mia Wasikowska, Iona Bell and Blake Harrison, with a screenplay written by Walliams and Kevin Cecil. It is directed by Australian filmmaker Jeffery Walker (Apple Cider Vinegar).

It is based on Walliams's 2019 book Fing. Williams has sold more than 60 million copies of his kids' books worldwide.

Fing! will retain its January 14 Australian release date, as confirmed by local distributor Transmission Films.

The cast of Fing!, director Jeffery Walker (far left) and co-writer Kevin Cecil (far right) at the film's Sundance premiere in January 2026. (Getty Images: Dia Dipasupil)

"Walliams will not be participating in the Australian publicity campaign," a Transmission Films spokesperson told ABC Arts.

"The campaign will focus on the film's Australian production, director and lead cast."

The fantasy family film follows parents tracking down a mythical beast to appease their unruly child. In addition to co-writing the screenplay, Walliams was set to feature in the film as a character called Headmaster.

"The film's producers have advised that they have removed Walliams's cameo appearance from Fing!" the Transmission spokesperson said.

Stan was slated to make Fing! available on its streaming platform following the movie's theatrical run, but has confirmed to ABC Arts it has been dropped.

"In light of the recent and serious allegations against David Walliams, Stan has removed Fing! from its content slate," a Stan spokesperson said.

The film's US distributor, Angel Studios, has also confirmed that it will be removing Walliams from the film.

"We take the allegations reported regarding David Walliams seriously," it said in a statement to Variety.

"Our thoughts are with anyone who has been affected ... and [Walliams] will have no involvement in the film's release or promotion."

UK distributor Sky has removed the film from its upcoming slate altogether.

"The allegations made against David Walliams are extremely serious," a spokesperson said.

"We have notified the producers of the film of our intention to exit our position as the UK and Ireland licensee of Fing."

Fifteen-year-old actor Iona Bell stars as Myrtle in Fing! (Supplied: Transmission)

Fing! was filmed in Queensland in 2025, with support from Screen Queensland.

"David Walliams's FING! is beloved by children around the world, and it's incredible to see our Production Attraction Strategy supporting renowned Queensland creatives as they bring it to life on the big screen," Queensland Arts Minister John-Paul Langbroek said in a press release at the time.

Screen Queensland said it was aware of media reports about Walliams.

"During production in early 2025, FING! generated more than $24 million in local expenditure and employed approximately 210 Queensland crew, as well as utilising small businesses to supply goods and services," a Screen Queensland spokesperson said.

"Screen Queensland assesses all applications for the Production Attraction Strategy incentive against a range of eligibility criteria including local expenditure and employment opportunities.

"The agency is not involved in production-specific decisions regarding cast and crew appointments or other matters such as distribution."

Walliams scrubbed by networks and publisher

The news about the Australian release of Fing! follows past Walliams projects, including Little Britain, being dropped from streaming services. The sketch show, which ran from 2003 to 2006, was nixed by its production company, the BBC, in 2020 amid concerns over its use of blackface.

David Walliams accused of grooming Actor, comedian and children's author David Walliams has been accused of allegedly grooming and preying on teenage girls in the early 2000s.

In 2020, the sketch show was removed from Stan, where it had been available to stream. It has also previously been available to watch on ABC iview.

A number of TV shows written by or starring Walliams, including a TV adaptation of his children's book Mr Stink, are also no longer available to watch on ABC iview.

"In light of the serious allegations against David Walliams, the ABC has removed some content from ABC iview," an ABC spokesperson said.

"We will continue to monitor developments."

Walliams was also a judge on Australia's Got Talent for its final season in 2022. Channel 7 has removed the season from its streaming platforms.

In December 2025, Walliams's publisher HarperCollins dropped the author after he faced accusations of harassing female staff, which he denied.

ABC News has approached HarperCollins for comment.

title: Foo Fighters' Grohl tribute for Beaconsfield mine 'hero'
text:
Foo Fighters leader Dave Grohl has paid tribute to Beaconsfield miner Todd Russell at the band's Sydney concert.

Russell died this week aged 54, days after leaving hospital to be with family, and 20 years after becoming internationally famous as a survivor of the Beaconsfield gold mine collapse, along with his colleague Brant Webb.

Loading...

On stage last night, Grohl told the Sydney crowd of the connection between the miners and his band.

"Back when Todd Russell and Brant Webb were stuck down there in the mine, someone from our record company called and said 'do you know about this mine collapse in Tasmania'?

"[I said] no, what's that?'

Dave Grohl explained to the crowd how the song came to be before performing it on acoustic guitar. (Supplied: Samantha Morando)

Grohl explained that he was told that the trapped men had asked for water "and an iPod with Foo Fighters music".

" I said 'no shit'! "

Grohl asked the record company to "send them a note [saying] 'hey, hope you guys are hanging in there, and when you get out, there are tickets to see the Foo Fighters play and let's have some beers'".

Loading...

Grohl told the Sydney audience that not long after the 2006 rescue, "we were playing the Opera House and I knew Brant Webb was coming … I wrote this in my hotel before the show", referring to the instrumental track The Ballad Of The Beaconsfield Miners.

Todd Russell remembered as a 'true-blue mate' Friends, community leaders and fellow Beaconsfield mine disaster survivor Brant Webb pay tribute to Todd Russell, who they say was a great mate and dedicated to his town.

He then explained that "afterwards we all went to the bar and we had the beers I promised; I got so drunk, I promised that I'd put this song on the next record. I am glad I did", referring to the band's 2007 album Echoes, Silence, Patience and Grace.

" I met a few heroes in my life, but that was a big one. I'm doing this for him tonight, Todd Russell. "

Grohl then performed the song solo on acoustic guitar.

Russell announced on social media last week that he was leaving hospital care to spend his last days at home.

He died days later, with his local community of Beaconsfield praising his decades of service as a firefighter.

title: Flexible school enrolments soar as families consider classroom alternatives
text:
For 16-year-old Joshua Houston, going to school used to mean wondering what might go wrong that day.

The Sunshine Coast teenager, who has Tourette syndrome, said he experienced bullying and disciplinary action at his former mainstream school.

"It felt like I was not heard and I felt like I was disrespected and no-one would really listen to me," he said.

Queensland senator Corinne Mulholland speaks with students at Kairos Community College in Nambour during a visit in August. (Supplied: Kairos Community College)

Now attending Kairos Community College in Nambour on the Sunshine Coast, Joshua says school has become somewhere he belongs.

"It feels like I've finally gotten to a point where I'm heard and that makes life even easier," he said.

"It feels like I've completed something in my life basically. And I've got a very good group of friends."

His experience comes as new research reveals enrolments at Queensland's independent special assistance schools have increased sevenfold since 2016, with more than 11,000 students attending schools in 2025.

The report, commissioned by Independent Schools Queensland (ISQ) and conducted by research firm McCrindle, also found principals were reporting extensive waiting lists.

'Big future'

Joshua's mother, Alicia Kerkow, said her son's Tourette syndrome was not always understood in mainstream education.

"He was always in trouble for things he couldn't control and things he couldn't help," she said.

By year 9, Joshua was barely attending school.

After initially trying a flexible learning program through Arethusa College, the family found Kairos.

Ms Kerkow said smaller classes, individual attention and a more flexible approach to assessments had helped Joshua regain confidence.

This year, he received an A in mathematics, something his mother said he had never achieved before.

"I do see a big future now," Joshua said.

For his mother, the transformation has been profound.

"He's happier. He's actually got dreams," she said.

Enrolments double in four years

The ISQ research found the number of independent special assistance schools increased from 14 in 2016 to 31 in 2025.

Separate figures from Queensland's Non-State Schools Accreditation Board show enrolments across the special assistance school sector more than doubled between 2022 and 2026.

Kairos Community College state principal Luke O'Sullivan said enrolment demand had also increased at his school, with waiting lists across its campuses for most year levels.

Luke O'Sullivan says students who once struggled are discovering new pathways for their futures. (Supplied: Kairos Community College)

Mr O'Sullivan said a new campus under construction at Nambour would further strengthen students' sense of belonging and safety.

"What we do isn't by chance, it is by design," he said.

An artist's impression of the new Kairos Community College campus at Nambour on the Sunshine Coast. (Supplied: Kairos Community College)

EREA Flexible Schools has grown from six schools in 2010 to 26 nationally, supporting more than 2,500 students.

Chief executive Matt Hawkins said continued funding was essential to meeting growing demand.

ISQ said special assistance schools mostly relied on government funding and did not charge tuition fees.

The ISQ research surveyed 271 former students and 410 parents of former students.

Three-quarters of surveyed parents said changing to a special assistance school had made a significant difference to their child's attendance, while 78 per cent said it had reduced pressure on their family.

Young women from EREA Flexible Schools in Brisbane attend a camp at Kooramindanjie (Carnarvon Gorge) with traditional owner Aunty Karen Lawton. (Supplied: EREA Flexi Schools)

The report estimated that helping approximately 2,000 students complete year 12 in 2025 could generate $452 million in lifetime fiscal benefits through increased tax revenue and reduced government expenditure.

The modelling compared the projected benefits of completing year 12 with leaving school early.

ISQ chief operating officer Stuart McDowall said the schools were changing young people's futures.

"Special assistance schools are not simply helping students stay in school," he said.

What mainstream schools could learn

Edith Cowan University education lecturer Jennifer Achari, who previously led an alternative school in Western Australia, said some students needed a different approach to learning.

Jennifer Achari says alternative schooling is booming in Queensland. (Supplied: Jennifer Achari)

"The schooling system is based on a standardised model of education, which is great for the majority of students," Dr Achari said.

"But for the students who are falling through the cracks and disengaging, they need a little bit of a different approach to education.

"Queensland is having the biggest boom at the minute [in alternative education] but there is a big huge increase across Australia."

Dr Achari said mainstream schools were also working to support students with diverse needs but could learn from the alternative sector's emphasis on belonging and building confidence.

"Hope was a huge one. That was actually the one that came out strongest in my research," Dr Achari said.

"Because the teachers have so much hope for their students."

For Joshua, that hope now extends beyond the classroom.

"If I put my mind to it, I can do whatever I want," he said.

The Queensland government has been contacted for comment.

title: David Jones's receiver reveals list of 19 stores set to close
text:
David Jones's receiver has confirmed it will close 19 of the retailer's 38 stores.

ABC News has also seen correspondence sent to staff and suppliers confirming the store closures.

The sites affected include a store in Sydney's Parramatta, three in Victoria and sites on the Gold Coast and Sunshine Coast in Queensland.

David Jones staff were sent a message this afternoon from chief executive Erica Berchtold about the "difficult news", which said a consultation period was about to begin for affected employees.

The ABC was sent a copy of it.

"I know how much our stores and the people in them mean to all of us, and this is difficult news for our whole business," Ms Berchtold wrote.

"We all know that the business could not continue operating as it was.

" Put simply, our store portfolio is no longer the right shape for the business. "

In a letter to suppliers, David Jones said: "We expect the affected stores to continue trading through the peak seasonal period, with closure dates anticipated to occur later in the year."

Stock at closing stores will be discounted or sent to other locations.

Do you know more? Email our journalist on terzon.emilia@abc.net.au or em.terzon@proton.me

'Slimline' David Jones an option

David Jones was placed in voluntary administration less than a week ago.

McGrathNicol was appointed as the voluntary administrator, acting on behalf of all the entities owed cash from its creditors.

Separately, FTI Consulting has been appointed as the receiver acting on behalf of David Jones's main secured lender, Hilco.

The collapse of the 188-year-old department store comes after negations with major landlord Westfield broke down, with the retailer's owner, Scentre Group, confirming David Jones had not paid rent since September in breach of its contracts.

Five outlets in Westfield shopping centres have already been flagged for closure due to them running at a loss, including Parramatta, Hornsby, Woden in Canberra, Carousel in Perth and Southland in Melbourne.

Loading...

Retail analyst Tom Kierath told ABC Business Daily that David Jones had "some wonderful sites", but it had too many.

He said parties interested in buying the business would likely be eyeing a smaller store footprint.

"I think the interest will be in a handful of sites rather than, necessarily the broader business," Mr Kierath, head of consumer research at Barrenjoey, said.

"Obviously some of the restructuring that's going on at the moment … if it does come back, it will come back in a much smaller, slimline version of it current self."

Analysts expect David Jones will focus on flagship stores such as Elizabeth Street in Sydney. (ABC News: Fletcher Yeung)

Mr Kierath said there was a place for a new-look version of David Jones, potentially with a focus on flagship stores with an enhanced offering.

"I think there's definitely a place for that, and with an enhanced food and beverage offering," he said.

"People are spending more and more out, and if you can make your stores a desirable place to hang out and spend time and eat and drink, that's another part of the offer that they can have.

"It probably needs to be reshaped a little bit. Obviously, smaller footprint with a bit more experience as opposed to huge spaces with not many staff."

Creditors given deadline to submit proof of debts

Many concession store shelves across David Jones stores were stripped of stock last week. (AAP: Eleanor Wilson)

Administrator McGrathNicol has given David Jones creditors until Monday to submit their proof of debt ahead of its first creditors meeting on Tuesday, which will be held remotely.

The call-out, which was sent with documents late on Tuesday afternoon, is likely to see thousands of small to large businesses come forward with claims, from fashion brands to major landlords.

There are now just days left for other entities to put in expressions of interest to buy David Jones.

David Jones has not paid rent on Westfield stores since September, according to owner Scentre Group. (ABC News)

McGrathNicol said it intended to lodge an application with the NSW Supreme Court to "extend the convening period, providing additional time to undertake a sale and/or recapitalisation process for David Jones Group".

It added that if the convening period was extended, the administrators' report to creditors and the second meeting of creditors would be held at a later date.

ABC News yesterday confirmed that David Jones was up to date with superannuation payments to its 6,000 employees, in line with new pay-day laws that came into effect in July.

title: Minjee Lee set to end horror 2026 season with Tour Championship absence
text:
Minjee Lee will miss the LPGA's rich and prestigious Tour Championship for the first time in more than a decade after calling an end to her deflating 2026 season.

Australia's triple major champion has opted out of The ANNIKA, the all-important penultimate event of the year starting on Thursday, rendering Lee no chance of scraping into next week's $US11 million ($16 million) showpiece in Florida.

Lee hasn't missed the season-ending championship since 2014.

But after slumping from third in the world rankings last October to 24th, her equal-lowest standing in 11 years, the WA superstar has opted for a reset following her last-place finish at the Japan Classic on Sunday.

Battling swing issues, the 30-year-old has slumped to 79th in the season-long point standings, with only the top 60 to qualify for the Tour Championship in Naples from November 19-22.

The 11-times LPGA Tour winner tied for 13th last year, with her best result in the event being a share of seventh on debut as a teenager in 2015.

While Lee will be absent this week, four Australians will be striving to punch their tickets to the Tour Championship at Pelican Golf Club in Belleair.

Perched safely in 11th place in the points race, Hannah Green is also sitting out The ANNIKA tournament.

But Cassie Porter (47th), Grace Kim (51st), Karis Davidson (54th) and Robyn Choi (61st) are all teeing it up.

Currently one spot outside the qualification zone, Choi likely needs a top-30 finish to clinch a maiden berth at the Tour Championship after enjoying a fruitful Asian swing.

Having become the first woman ever to clinch player-of-the-year honours before the Tour Championship, world No.1 Nelly Korda is chasing more history this week.

The American can become the first LPGA professional to win the same event for the fourth time since The ANNIKA tournament namesake Annika Sorenstam in 2005.

Korda also has a chance to become the fifth player in LPGA Tour history to win the same tournament at least four times and the first since Se Ri Pak at the Jamie Farr Kroger Classic in 2003.

AAP

title: Advocacy group ordered to destroy abattoir video footage by High Court
text:
An animal rights group that planted cameras around a Victorian goat abattoir has won a High Court challenge over who owns the rights to the covertly captured video footage, but the court has ordered it to destroy the recordings.

Farm Transparency International (FTI) said it was extremely disappointed by the outcome, which it said would stifle the public’s right to know what happens inside slaughterhouses.

The case involved a director and an employee from FTI who secretly installed cameras at a halal abattoir in Eurobin, in north-east Victoria.

They admitted to trespassing onto the property, owned by Game Meats Company of Australia (GMC), seven times between January and April 2024.

With the footage, FTI put together a 14-minute video of what they described as "extreme animal cruelty".

Farm Transparency International executive director Chris Delforce said the instruction to destory the footage was disappointing. (Supplied: Farm Transparency International)

But when they sent it to the federal regulator, a local television news station, and posted it online, the abattoir headed to the Federal Court.

The activists were ordered to pay $130,000 in damages.

GMC also won an injunction which ordered the online footage to be taken down.

Questions about who should own the footage were only taken up on appeal, when the court determined that ownership was allocated to the abattoir, not the activists who collected it.

The court used a mechanism called a "constructive trust" to assign ownership to GMC.

It is a remedy imposed by a court when property arises from wrongdoing, but it has never been applied to such a copyright case before.

Copyright concerns

The notion of the "constructive trust" was at the heart of the activists' High Court challenge.

They argued that the court's reasoning was flawed because it did not identify a principle or properly identify facts that supported the decision.

They said that while the trespass was wrong, the act of making the video recordings was separate and was not wrong.

The activists also said a lesser remedy would have been enough without requiring the rights of the footage to be allocated to the abattoir.

On the other hand, the abattoir argued the trespasses engaged in by FTI were "among the most obvious examples of intentional wrongdoing that one might imagine."

They submitted that even without a trust, the court should have granted an injunction that would have prevented the footage from being published and protected GMC from any ongoing consequences.

Activists 'extremely disappointed'

The High Court unanimously allowed the appeal by FTI in part, meaning the activists have been successful in their claim that no constructive trust should be declared over its copyright in the images.

The court found that the rights conferred to GMC through the constructive trust could be used to prevent the further dissemination of the images by people outside of FTI.

"Exercise of those rights against those persons would involve separate and subsequent proceedings against those persons for breach of copyright," the judgment said.

"The potential impact on the common law freedom of communication of those persons, and in turn on political communication and on the public interest in free speech, cannot be ignored and cannot be gainsaid."

The High Court ruled in favour of FTI but ordered it to destroy the recordings. (ABC News)

However, the High Court ruled FTI must destroy all recordings and copies obtained as a result of its trespasses.

"Justice is best served by the more limited remedy of the injunction against Farm Transparency requiring deletion of the images," the court said.

In a statement, FTI executive director Chris Delforce said the organisation was "extremely disappointed" by the judgment.

"While we're glad the copyright claim on the footage has been defeated, and that third parties such as media outlets are not restricted from publishing, the order for us to destroy all copies of the footage means that only those third parties that downloaded the footage in the few hours that it was published on 17 May 2024 will have any way of publishing it now," Mr Delforce said.

"This is an enormous blow to the public's right to know what happens in slaughterhouses and factory farms.

"We will comply with the orders and delete all copies of the footage in our possession, but we will never stop fighting against cruelty and injustice."

title: See which incomes are hit hardest by tax bracket creep
text:
Workers who earn the minimum wage and those who are on the cusp of the top tax bracket are the hardest hit by bracket creep, according to new research.

The federal opposition wants to stamp out the longstanding feature of Australia's tax system, where people see larger proportions of their incomes taxed over time.

It occurs because tax brackets do not move with inflation, so people "creep" into higher brackets.

Analysis by the e61 Institute and economist Richard Holden has found that workers earning about $45,000 and those earning about $190,000 are penalised the most by bracket creep, largely because their incomes are on the cusp of higher brackets.

Over a decade from 2028, someone who currently earns $45,000 would face an increase of more than five percentage points in their average tax rate. This level is close to the full-time minimum wage, although many part-timers also earn in this range.

Over the same period, someone who currently earns $190,000 would face an increase of more than four percentage points. In both of these cases, more than half of a person's real income growth would be taxed.

While those two groups are the worst affected, the vast majority of taxpayers would face a hike of at least two percentage points and see at least a quarter of their real income growth taxed.

Income today Average tax today Average tax in 10yrs $45,000 11% 16% $75,000 20% 22% $100,000 23% 25% $190,000 29% 34% $300,000 36% 39%

"Taxing workers more without explicit policy change is neither an equitable nor a credible mechanism for [raising revenue]," e61 chief executive Michael Brennan said.

"The tax increase falls unevenly across the income distribution."

Budget claims of 'return to surplus' rely on bracket creep

In practice, the scenario e61 uses is unlikely to play out because it assumes there are no income tax cuts for a full decade.

As history shows, governments almost always cut taxes every few years, often close to elections, "handing back" some or all of the bracket creep.

Over several decades, these tax cuts have served to keep average tax rates broadly stable, albeit in an irregular and uneven way.

But the authors note that this same unlikely assumption is used in the government's own budget projections, helping successive treasurers to claim that the budget is on track to return to surplus, when this would not be true without bracket creep.

Analysis by the independent Parliamentary Budget Office shows the budget would have a deficit equivalent to 0.7 per cent of GDP (the size of the economy) by the end of the decade without bracket creep, contrary to the official projection of a 1 per cent surplus.

"Bracket creep should not be treated as a serious long-run funding strategy," the authors wrote. "Fiscal projections that implicitly assume it will repair the budget are not credible."

Coalition bid to index tax brackets

Opposition Leader Angus Taylor has pledged to index tax brackets to inflation if elected, phased in over two years from 2028.

The proposal would result in bracket creep being paid back to taxpayers as a lump sum at the end of each tax year, based on the level of inflation.

The opposition said the budgetary cost of the tax cuts could be met in the first three years by its proposed cuts to Labor's climate and housing policies and industry subsidies, and by scrapping Labor's $250 tax offset for wage earners.

Over the longer term, Mr Taylor has suggested the cost to the budget would be met by limiting government spending, prompting accusations from Labor that the Coalition would be forced into unspecified and damaging spending cuts to fund its plans.

Loading...

Economist Saul Eslake told the ABC that, while he supported indexing tax brackets in principle and that doing so would impose greater honesty on governments, he was doubtful governments could find the spending cuts to balance it out.

"I don't believe what the Coalition says about how much they're going to save over time. It's been evident since Josh Frydenberg's last budget that government spending was set to be higher than the average which had prevailed for decades," he said.

"That's for three reasons. The public clearly wants more aged, disability and health care … and there's a bipartisan consensus that whether the public wants it or not, they're going to get more spending on defence.

"And thirdly, as a result of deficits run up since the global financial crisis [in 2008] and because we're no longer living in the world of ultra-low interest rates, we're going to have to spend a lot more on interest.

"If you take those three areas and also add spending on pension and benefits, which I don't think anyone wants to cut, and the revenue from the GST that has to go to the states, you're talking about 67 per cent of federal spending."

Mr Eslake said governments had not been willing "to have an honest conversation with the public that if we want all this, we have to have more tax".

The e61 researchers also acknowledged the spending pressures coming from care and other areas, but said bracket creep could not be the solution to this problem.

"The two credible paths to fiscal sustainability are deliberate moderation in the growth of public spending, and tax reform to raise revenue in a more sustainable and less distortive way than bracket creep," Mr Brennan said.

title: Cooped-up free-range hens set free again as bird flu spread slows in SA
text:
Three months after South Australian egg farmers were given the voluntary order to put their free-range chooks in lockdown, some producers are setting their hens free again.

In August, Riverland egg farmer Darren Letton was among those who took the precautionary step to lock his hens inside.

The deadly H5N1 virus had been detected in wild birds several weeks earlier, and the number of confirmed cases was quickly climbing.

Darren Letton operates Glenview Poultry Farm at Pike River, in SA's Riverland. (ABC Riverland: Shannon Pearce)

But now, as those cases dwindle, Mr Letton has released his chooks — albeit with some reluctance.

While the poultry industry has not reported any cases of bird flu in any agricultural settings across Australia, there is still some risk.

"Having a voluntary order allowed us to make that decision for ourselves, so a couple of weeks after [that] I decided to lock up my birds," Mr Letton said.

"Last week I decided it was time to let the birds out again.

" I feel like it's OK for the moment, hopefully. "

It is a choice facing many of the state's free-range egg and poultry producers, with the SA government's voluntary housing recommendation for free-range poultry still in place and scheduled to run until November 20.

Shoppers have probably noticed the "temporarily housed" stickers on free-range chicken in recent months. (ABC Rural: Alana Calvert)

"I've talked to a few other producers about it," Mr Letton said.

"Some [chooks] are still locked up, some can't [be] and some [farmers] have decided they'd just weigh the cost of it."

Packaging cost concerns

Aside from the slowing spread of bird flu across SA, Mr Letton said his decision was also based on the potential cost of having to change his free-range packaging if he continued to house his hens.

As a result of H5N1 spreading to Australia, the Australian Consumer and Competition Commission (ACCC) issued guidance allowing farmers to keep chickens indoors and still use free-range cartons.

Darren Letton says the decision to let his hens back out was not easy. (ABC News: Sophie Holder)

It means the ACCC will not take enforcement action against producers marketing their eggs or poultry meat as free-range if they are affected by a mandatory housing order or voluntary housing recommendation for up to 90 days.

Beyond that time, producers need to provide alternative labelling for consumers.

"It's not an easy thing to do," Mr Letton said.

"A lot of us have free-range egg cartons; we don't have barn-laid cartons — you can't just produce them overnight."

The ACCC has issued guidance for free-range egg farmers who are housing their hens. (ABC Rural: Justine Longmore)

Mr Letton said he would "keep an eye" on the virus's spread, fearing that if it did reach his flock, it would decimate his business.

"I'm thinking, 'How much longer can I do this without going broke, without it happening?'" he said.

"Because if it happens, that'll be the thing that makes me decide to get out of the industry."

SA spread slows

SA's chief veterinarian Skye Fruean said the state had recorded 342 bird flu cases as of Monday, but detections had slowed in recent weeks.

She said she was "not necessarily" surprised by that trend.

"We don't have a crystal ball, so we never knew where this was going to go," Dr Fruean said.

Skye Fruean says H5 bird flu is still spreading. (ABC News: Simon Goodes)

"Our MO was to plan for the worst and hope for the best, and it's very pleasing to see that the numbers do seem to be decreasing, but we only need it to spill into a new species for it to potentially take off again, so we do need to keep that surveillance effort up.

" We're pretty confident the amount of spread has tailed off a little bit, but it certainly hasn't gone away completely. "

Dr Fruean said her advice to the state's egg and poultry producers to consider housing their free-range birds was constantly being reviewed, but had not changed.

"The reason is that the risk is still there," she said.

"It is very pleasing that we haven't had any detections in the poultry sector, and I certainly hope it stays that way, [but] what we've learned from overseas is that we can probably expect that to happen at some point in time.

SA's poultry and egg producers have been asked to consider housing their free-range chickens as bird flu spreads. (ABC News: Steven Schubert)

"That's what we and the poultry industry are planning for, to prevent that as much as we can.

"Broadly, the advice is a precautionary measure — keep your chooks inside if it's feasible and safe to do so.

"We need to take into consideration the biosecurity risk, but also considerations such as welfare, so we're not encouraging everyone to lock up their chooks without considering those other factors."

title: Warner jabs former Australian coach Lehmann over Sandpapergate sanctions
text:
David Warner has fired an indirect jab at Darren Lehmann, suggesting the ex-Australian coach knew of the use of sandpaper in the 2018 ball-tampering scandal.

Warner agreed with former International Cricket Council match referee Chris Broad, who said that Lehmann must have known of Australia's use of sandpaper on the ball, and if he did not, then he should not have been coach.

"Darren Lehmann surely knew all about it," Broad told Track Radio.

"And if he didn't, he shouldn't have been the coach at the time.

"He has got away lightly because he, OK, he left his job a few months later, but he didn't get any sanctions."

Warner replied to Track Radio's social media post of Broad's comments, writing on X: "I couldn't agree more and that's hard for me to say!"

Lehmann, who stepped down as Australia's coach in the aftermath of the 2018 scandal in South Africa, has denied personal knowledge of the Test team using sandpaper on the ball.

"I don't think everyone would have known [about the use of sandpaper]. You do know ball tampering is going on because it's been happening for 150 years," Lehmann, who will co-host the ABC's cricket podcast this season, told Summer Grandstand on the weekend.

"It's just how it's being done, and how you would know to that extent? That's an individual case-by-case, to be fair.

"I can only speak to what I know, and I know ball tampering was a big part of the game of cricket. Now it is obsolete.

Loading...

"That doesn't make it right either, but that's the case, and we paid a heavy price for that."

Lehmann's comments are at odds with Usman Khawaja's claims the whole team knew of the sandpaper plans, and the illegal tactic was also used in the match prior to being uncovered by television cameras at the infamous 2018 Test in Cape Town.

Cricket Australia (CA) has ruled out reopening its investigation into the scandal.

Warner on Monday night backed Khawaja's claims, labelling CA's investigation as "rushed and botched" after it found only he, Cameron Bancroft and Steve Smith knew of the plan.

CA banned Smith and Warner from playing any cricket for one year and also suspended Bancroft for nine months. Smith and Warner were also stripped of their respective captain and vice-captain roles.

Paceman Mitchell Starc repeated his denial of the sandpaper plot when he became the first player from the match to front media, citing a statement he and his fellow bowlers made in 2021.

Usman Khawaja's (left) claims that everyone knew about the use of sandpaper has been backed by David Warner (second from left), denied by Darren Lehmann (right), while Steve Smith (second from right) is yet to comment. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

"We [bowlers] weren't aware anything was taken on to the field to be tampered with," Starc said on Tuesday.

"We saw [the sandpaper] on the big screen in Cape Town."

Asked why he and Khawaja had differing views, Starc responded: "That's a question for him."

"I'll stick to what I said … at the time, eight years ago. Clearly, there's different versions from different people."

Australian Cricketers Association chief executive Paul Marsh said on Tuesday it was understandable players' versions of events could differ.

Loading...

"Players and staff at the heart of the issue are entitled to share their experiences, just as others are entitled to put such a challenging period in their life behind them," Marsh said in a statement.

"There are no winners in this issue, and nothing can undo what happened.

"But we must recognise that there are humans in the centre of this and we are calling for the ongoing vitriol directed at those involved to come to an end."

Marsh's statement attracted the ire of former Test batsman Damien Martyn, who posted on X: "This statement from our players union does not reflect all ex players' opinions."

Meanwhile, the author of a review into Australia's cricket culture said he may have been lied to by players.

Simon Longstaff led an Ethics Centre team tasked with examining the sport's culture, but not the sandpaper scandal itself.

"Those matters had been investigated by Cricket Australia, and the findings were concluded," Longstaff wrote in the Australian Financial Review on Wednesday.

"Even so, we picked up whispers — few and very faint — that, perhaps, the public record did not tell the full story.

"All I can say is that if what Khawaja alleges turns out to be true, then I was also lied to.

"It is easy enough to understand how a group of players might perpetuate — either by act or omission — what could turn out to be a lie."

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

AAP

title: China hits $US1 trillion trade surplus as exports to US surge
text:
China's trade surplus ballooned to more than $US1 trillion ($1.4 trillion) in the 10 months to October, official data shows, with the country reaching the milestone even earlier than 2025's record-breaking sum.

The figures come ahead of talks between China President Xi Jinping and his US counterpart Donald Trump at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in China next week, when trade tensions will likely loom large.

Exports from the world's second-largest economy have surged in recent months, driven in part by soaring global demand for AI-related products including computer chips, data centre servers and networking equipment.

The trade boom has offered Beijing a key economic lifeline as domestic activity is weighed down by longstanding woes in the once-roaring property sector.

Exports jumped 35.2 per cent year-on-year to $US412.3 billion last month, according to the General Administration of Customs (GAC), while imports expanded 41.6 per cent to $US307.1 billion.

The figures brought China's total trade surplus during the first 10 months to a towering $US1.04 trillion, according to the GAC.

Trade has been a key issue for Xi Jinping and Donald Trump in recent years. (Reuters: Kylie Cooper)

"Exporters have been the key driving force behind China's economy this year," Zhiwei Zhang, president and chief economist at Pinpoint Asset Management, wrote.

"I expect they will continue to perform well in the foreseeable future," he said, adding that he did not think China's macro policy stance would change significantly for the rest of the year.

The country is well on track to surpass the record $US1.2 trillion surplus hit last year, when the $US1 trillion mark was reached in November.

However, the export boom has fuelled tensions with several key trading partners, who complain that floods of lower-cost Chinese goods are doing huge damage to their local industries.

Chinese exports to US grow

In unwelcome news to Washington, the latest figures show Chinese exports to the United States surged 32.9 per cent last month.

Mr Xi and Mr Trump have navigated a shaky truce to a fierce trade war since their meeting in October last year, agreeing recently to extend the arrangement ahead of talks that were held in Washington in September.

They are expected to hold another head-to-head at the APEC gathering, which runs from November 18 to 19 in Shenzhen and could also see the pair meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin for trilateral talks.

China, US agree to AI dialogue, tariff cuts The tariff reductions will apply to US exports, such as agricultural goods, wood and cosmetics.

On Friday, top Chinese and US officials held what readouts suggested were tetchy talks ahead of the summit.

The Americans stressed "the importance of China fully and immediately implementing its commitments" and highlighted "concerns about recent Chinese actions", according to the US Treasury Department.

Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng expressed "serious concerns over recent economic and trade restrictive measures imposed by the United States", according to a state media report.

Trade frictions with EU continue

China's trade surplus with the European Union has also rankled Brussels.

Tuesday's data showed China's surplus with the 27-nation bloc had swelled to $US310.7 billion in January-October, topping the $US241.6 billion recorded during the same period last year.

Talks last month in Beijing between EU trade chief Maros Sefcovic and Chinese counterpart Wang Wentao ended with an agreement to limit exports of hybrid vehicles to Europe.

"Trade frictions with the EU have continued to broaden in recent weeks," wrote Nguyen Hoang Nam of Capital Economics.

Steps taken recently by Brussels to stem the flow of imports, including 2-euro fees on all packages entering the bloc, "so far cover only a small portion of China's exports and are unlikely to have much impact on the economy", Mr Nguyen said.

Analysts say Beijing is relying heavily on exports to achieve its official growth target for this year of 4.5-5.0 per cent, its lowest goal in decades.

Domestic consumption has been sluggish for several years, with data on Monday showing inflation was still well short of the official target of about 2 per cent.

AFP

We know the social media formula: two ingredients + surprise and delight = a viral recipe hit. We just love the promise of a budget-friendly recipe that somehow delivers more than the sum of its parts for an unreasonably delicious result. And here’s the latest contender – two-ingredient “button” noodles that act as the bounciest sauce delivery system we’ve come across yet. Satisfyingly squidgy: carrot and beetroot button noodles. Jane de Graaff In a continuation of the potato noodle trend (cooked potato mixed with potato starch and using a bottleneck to create a “mushroom” shape), the latest iteration subs out the potato for various root vegies and a thumbprint for more colourful results. We’ve seen variations from beetroot to carrot and the dish itself has been called everything from “button noodles” to Korean-style gnocchi. But does it live up to the viral ooohs and aaahs creators lather it with? Does it work The premise of the recipe is simple. Steam carrot/beetroot/sweet potato/pumpkin until fall-apart soft. Mash smooth and mix with starch (glutinous rice flour/potato starch/tapioca flour) to make a soft and easy-to-handle dough. Roll it into little balls, press with your thumb to create a “button” shape, then boil until they bob to the surface of your bubbling pot, drain and serve drenched in chilli-garlic sauce of your choice. Popular versions have been shared by creators including Dan Dumbrell and Itsvegansis.

Advertisement

“I was a bit of a sceptic going in,” says cookbook author, sweet expert and creator of viral food content Catherine Zhang. “A noodle made from mashed potato and potato starch sounds like it should be gluey, but the first batch came out bouncy and slippery, somewhere between tteokbokki rice cakes and a thick udon. What won me over was the little dimple in the middle. It’s a tiny cup, so every piece carries its own pool of chilli oil.” The best recipes from Australia's leading chefs straight to your inbox. Sign up Why do we love it It’s a new riff on an old idea, simplified and made hyper-accessible by content creators for home cooks. “Starch and a cooked root vegetable kneaded into a chewy dough exists all over Asia,” says Zhang.

Advertisement

“In Taiwan, there are taro balls and sweet potato balls of mashed root plus tapioca starch served in sweet soups – which is where I come at this from, as a dessert person. “Hokkaido has imo mochi, mashed potato and potato starch pressed into discs and pan fried. Korea has gamja ongsimi — potato dumplings in soup. Northern China has pressed thumb pastas like cat’s ear noodles, and Italy has gnocchi, which is the same logic with wheat flour. “So the social media version is really a mash-up: a Taiwanese taro ball dough, shaped like a Chinese thumb pasta in a Sichuan-style chilli oil sauce. I just call them button noodles, because that’s what everyone searches for, though at home they get called ‘the chewy potato ones’.” While Zhang says they hit the viral big time because of their two-ingredient 20-minute ease and their built-for-video so-satisfying visuals, it’s the texture and the sauce that really seal the deal. “There’s a whole generation obsessed with chew: boba, mochi doughnuts, tteokbokki ... Button noodles are that ‘QQ’ bounce in its purest form,” she says, referring to the term some cultures in East Asia use to describe that satisfyingly squidgy texture.

Advertisement

The sauce is also a long-time winner: a combination of chilli, garlic, soy, vinegar, spring onion and hot oil sizzled over the top. “The noodle changed, the sauce did not. So people already knew they would like it. The carrot and pumpkin versions kept it going because colour is a free hook.” Is it worth making? The short answer is yes. The bouncy little delicious results shift between slippery or chewy depending on your flour choice, with Zhang recommending the glutinous rice flour version. “My honest verdict: they are more of a dumpling than a noodle, they are very moreish, and they are at their best in the first 10 minutes out of the pot.”

Advertisement

Yes, they are as easy to make as the social videos claim. They look great, and that little divot made by your thumbprint is a perfect sauce-pooling point. Pro tips for making them at home Knead only a little – you’re not working gluten and over-handling dries them out.

Mash the root vegies while hot and add your starch straight away to start the cooking process – it helps with structure.

Work with weights rather than cup measures – Zhang recommends 2 parts cooked root vegie to 1 part starch by weight, adjusted by feel to avoid crumbly or gluey textures.

Keep your buttons small so they cook through.

Boil them hard and leave them in for an extra minute after they float.

Rinse them under cold water to tighten the chew.

Drench them in sauce as soon as they’re ready – they’re best eaten fresh, but can be revived in a little boiling water. Zhang’s notes on starch types Potato starch is a more classic version for a clear, bouncy, slippery result.

Glutinous rice flour gives a softer, more tender mochi chew, and it is the easiest dough to handle, but has a less glassy texture.

Tapioca is the stretchiest and most translucent but becomes gummy very quickly, so is best in a blend.

Advertisement

Two-ingredient carrot and beetroot button noodles. Jane de Graaff Viral carrot and beetroot button noodles This easy and eye-catching recipe is best when you make a batch of each of the carrot and beet versions and mix them together for a rainbow result. INGREDIENTS 400g carrot or beetroot, peeled and large diced

200g glutinous rice flour + extra

pinch of salt

Advertisement

Sauce ingredients 2 spring onions, very finely chopped

¼ cup coriander leaves, finely chopped

2 tsp garlic paste

¼ tsp chilli flakes

1 tsp caster sugar

3 tbsp sweet soy sauce

1 tbsp black vinegar

½ tsp sesame oil

2 tbsp rice bran or peanut oil OR 2 tbsp chilli crisp oil METHOD

Advertisement

First, prepare all your sauce ingredients: finely slice spring onion, coriander and garlic. Mix together soy sauce, black vinegar and sesame oil. Next, make your noodles. Peel and cut your carrot or beetroot into small pieces. Cover with water and a pinch of salt and bring to the boil, simmering for 10 minutes or until completely tender and mashable with a fork. Drain, and while still hot, mash your carrot or beetroot until very smooth. When just cool enough to handle (but still hot) add the glutinous rice flour and knead into a smooth dough. If it’s too sticky or a little crumbly, adjust it with a little more glutinous rice flour or water until it can be easily rolled into a smooth ball. Bring a large pot of water to the boil. Break off small pieces of the dough, roll into small balls and then press with your thumb to create a button shape. Repeat until all the dough is used. Add the buttons to the boiling pot and cook until they all bob to the surface, then cook for 1 extra minute. Drain and run under cold or icy water to tighten the noodles for extra bounce. In a small pot, heat your rice bran or peanut oil until boiling. Put your cooked noodles into a bowl and add spring onion, coriander, garlic, chilli flakes, caster and sugar. Pour over the hot oil for a sizzle, then add the vinegar soy mix and toss through. Serve immediately.
