Orbit Resources has fired up the drill rig for a second stage of partner-funded diamond campaign at its Goodrich Porphyry prospect, 70 kilometres south-west of Orange, within the highly prospective Lachlan Fold Belt in New South Wales. The four-hole, 1000-metre program follows July’s stage-one discovery of the aptly named “Pencil Porphyry” - a narrow, vertically extensive mineralised structure - which delivered a solid hit of 136.55m grading 0.32 per cent copper, 0.16 grams per tonne (g/t) gold and 43g/t molybdenum from 81.45m. That intercept also contained a richer 3.55-metre core running at an impressive 2.8 per cent copper. Orbit Resources has begun a new diamond drilling program at its Goodrich copper-gold project in New South Wales. Geologically, the company’s initial discovery was a textbook hit, intersecting a chalcopyrite-bearing monzonite porphyry. The intrusion also exhibited mineralised “unidirectional solidification textures”, key pathfinders for large ore systems, suggesting the ground may hold further treasures lurking below. The new drilling will test the lateral and down-dip extent of the interpreted porphyry system and investigate its continuity with historical copper-gold intercepts associated with the project’s nearby Goodrich open pit.

Advertisement

‘Stage two drilling is now underway and is designed to test how far the existing porphyry extends.’ Orbit Resources managing director Jeneta Owens Orbit’s joint venture partner, Canadian-listed Great Plains Metals Corp, is fully funding the program and is now providing an additional $1 million of work, including a minimum of 500m of drilling under the joint venture agreement as it works towards earning a 70 per cent stake. The deal will leave Orbit holding a 30 per cent interest, giving it cost-effective exposure to further exploration success without having to foot the bill during the earn-in period. Orbit Resources managing director Jeneta Owens said: “Stage-one drilling at Goodrich returned a broad interval of copper-gold-molybdenum mineralisation from relatively shallow depth. Stage-two drilling is now underway and is designed to test how far the existing porphyry extends, and whether it connects with the shallower historical copper-gold intercepts around the Goodrich open pit.” While the JV drilling at Goodrich provides a free kick at goal, Orbit’s main game remains its flagship Lewis Ponds gold-silver-zinc project, also in the Lachlan Fold Belt. The project already hosts a hefty mineral resource of 17.52 million tonnes (Mt) containing 1.7 million ounces of gold equivalent. A scoping study on Lewis Ponds outlined a robust base-case pre-tax net present value (NPV) of $481 million, using gold at US$3700 (A$5410) an ounce and silver at US$55 (A$80) an ounce. However, an upside case based on February spot prices of US$5055 (A$7390) gold and US$82 (A$120) silver sent the potential economics into the stratosphere, delivering a pre-tax NPV of a whopping $1.088 billion and a 40 per cent internal rate of return.

Advertisement

Adding to the project’s credentials, recent drilling at its Spicer’s Lode appears to have opened up some serious exploration upside after the final hole of a recent four-hole resource development campaign intersected a thick 28.1-metre zone of visual sulphide mineralisation, including sections with up to 34 per cent semi-massive sulphides. While visual estimates are no substitute for assays, the core showed a polymetallic sulphide assemblage of pyrite, sphalerite, galena, chalcopyrite and pyrrhotite. Assays from the lab are pending. The company has also defined a new discovery at Cousin Jack, roughly 350m southeast of the main Lewis Ponds resource, with initial drilling hitting encouraging base metal grades, including a 1.7-metre section containing 11.35% zinc, 0.34% copper and 18.05g/t silver from 585m. Rounding out Orbit’s portfolio is the Narraburra rare earths project, 250km southwest of its flagship Lewis Ponds. The ionic-clay rare earths deposit hosts a maiden JORC-compliant resource of 94.9 million tonnes (Mt) grading 739 parts per million (ppm) total rare earth oxides, including a higher-grade core of 20Mt at 1079ppm. With its JV partner footing the bill to chase a promising porphyry discovery at Goodrich and a suite of potentially company-making assets in its own right, Orbit appears to have engineered multiple streams of news flow. While the Goodrich work unfolds, all eyes will be on the pending assays from Lewis Ponds to see if the visual sulphide hits can deliver the grades needed to edge the potential billion-dollar project closer to reality. title: Cricket Australia must get to the bottom of what happened in South Africa
text:

SportCricketAustralian cricket Editorial Cricket Australia must get to the bottom of what happened in South Africa The Herald's View Editorial November 11, 2026 — 3:59pm

November 11, 2026 — 3:59pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The smell that has wafted around Cricket Australia’s brusque response to cheating by the Australian team in South Africa eight years ago has redeveloped into a strong stench blanketing officialdom’s claim that the matter is closed. Cricket Australian offered up three sacrificial lambs after Cameron Bancroft was filmed shoving sandpaper into his pants. Bancroft was banned for nine months. Skipper Steve Smith and batsman Dave Warner received 12-month suspensions. Smith was banned also from the captaincy for at least two years, while Warner was told he would never lead Australia. Usman Khawaja has written about the sandpaper scandal in his new autobiography. Dan Peled One of Australia’s players in that Cape Town Test, Usman Khawaja, who retired last January, has written an autobiography, Sabr, in which he claims the entire team knew of tampering with the ball in the previous Port Elizabeth Test. “It was all of us. Not the batters, not the bowlers, not the staff. All of us,” Khawaja told the Herald. Warner has come out and said Kawaaja’s recollection was 100 per cent accurate.“Now everyone knows the truth. It’s out there. People wanted to know it. You’ve come out and said it.”

Advertisement

Related Article Australian cricket Sandpaper feuds erupt: Warner takes on ex-coach Lehmann in stunning twist Mitchell Starc is the first current player to deny the allegations, saying his recollection hadn’t changed over time and his fellow bowlers knew nothing about the sandpaper use. In 2021, when the controversy re-erupted, four of the Australian bowlers in Cape Town Test, Pat Cummins, Josh Hazlewood, Mitch Starc and Nathan Lyon, released a statement re-affirming that they did not know a “foreign substance was taken onto the field to alter the condition of the ball” until they saw images of the sandpaper in Bancroft’s possession on the big screen at the ground. The sport personifies ethics and fair play; the official rulebook includes a preamble called the “Spirit of Cricket”. However, there has long been tension between the romanticised ideal and the pressure of professionalism. The 1932-33 “Bodyline” series shocked Australia when England bowled lethal bouncers, and a 1981 one-day international turned into national shame after Australian captain Greg Chappell instructed his younger brother, Trevor, to roll the final delivery underarm to prevent New Zealand from hitting a six to win the match. The same infamy haunts Sandpapergate.

Advertisement

Related Article Australian cricket Khawaja cancels book interviews after refusing to answer key question about Cummins Simon Longstaff, who led a review into the culture of Cricket Australia in 2018, said he had heard whispers that the public record of the cheating scandal was inaccurate and a cover-up was possible. “All I can say is that if what Khawaja alleges turns out to be true, then I was also lied to,” Longstaff wrote in the Australian Financial Review. Khawaja has pulled out of promotional media interviews after being challenged to comment on other players’ reactions to his claims. Cricket Australia has ruled out reopening an investigation into Sandpapergate. It is a predictable self-protection ignoring the uncomfortable reality that five players who played in South Africa are expected to feature in the Test squad to play New Zealand this summer and the likelihood the scandal will fester for years as others release their own biographies.

Advertisement

Cricket Australia needs to recognise that their sport personifies ethics and fair play, both on the field and the boardroom. It needs to get to the bottom of what happened in South Africa once and for all, for the good of the game. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. PoliticsFederalNegative gearing Record plunge in investor loans as tax overhaul hits property market Shane Wright Updated November 11, 2026 — 3:53pm ,first published 3:48pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. The federal government’s budget overhaul of negative gearing and capital gains tax has been blamed for the biggest fall in home loans taken out by investors on record, with warnings the property market will struggle well into next year. Figures from the Australian Bureau of Statistics released this morning showed loans to investors dropped by 30.6 per cent in the three months to September. Over the past 12 months, investor loans are down by 38.6 per cent. The number of investor loans for existing homes in NSW has tumbled by up to 50 per cent over the past three months. Jessica Shapiro The drop, however, is concentrated among investors who purchase existing homes. In NSW, investor loans for new builds fell by 18.4 per cent through the September quarter but for existing dwellings they collapsed by almost 50 per cent. It was a similar story across the rest of the country. Loans by investors for existing homes fell by 27 per cent in Victoria, by 40 per cent in Queensland and by 38.1 per cent in Western Australia.

Advertisement

Nationally, the ratio of investors buying existing homes to building new properties fell to its lowest level on record. The sharp falls occurred after the May budget in which Treasurer Jim Chalmers revealed plans to limit negative gearing - the ability to offset losses on a rental property against a person’s total income - to new builds from July 1 next year. The 50 per cent capital gains tax concession, blamed by critics for the step-up in property prices and investor activity after it was introduced by the Howard government, will return to an inflation-adjusted basis on July 1 next year. The changes were announced after the Reserve Bank began lifting interest rates and the start of a fall in national property prices now in its seventh consecutive month.

Advertisement

Overall new home loans fell by 15.5 per cent through the quarter to be 21.4 per cent down over the past year. This included first home buyers with loans to new entrants to the property market falling 8.6 per cent in the quarter and 12.3 per cent over the year. Housing Minister Clare O’Neil said the figures showed a clear shift away from investors towards people wanting to buy their own home and that investors had moved towards constructing new houses. Related Article Property prices Air is coming out of the housing bubble. Is now the time for first home buyers? “We’ve had a housing market geared towards investors for a generation, and where did it get us? Plummeting home ownership, out-of-control house price increases, and a generation losing hope,” she told this masthead. “These numbers show the balance is shifting back towards Australians who are buying a home to live in, and especially to our first home buyers.”

Advertisement

Liberal housing spokesman Andrew Bragg said the figures showed the government’s tax policies were hurting the property market and homeowners. “No one wins from the new taxes, not first homeowners, not owners, not renters and not investors. Time for them to be repealed,” he said. JP Morgan economist Tom Ryan noted that the drop in lending to owner-occupiers was in line with other falls during periods when the Reserve Bank was tightening monetary policy. But the drop in investor lending was being exacerbated by the tax changes in this year’s budget, with Ryan warning that they are “likely to remain a structural drag” for some time.

Advertisement

HIA senior economist Maurice Tapang said the lift in business construction may mean that builders are constructing spec housing to protect their sub-contractors. He said the property sector had yet to feel the full brunt of the RBA’s five rate hikes and the blow to confidence dealt by the government’s tax changes. “Investors are crucial to addressing the housing under-supply and moderating downward cycles in the market. They add to rental supply and net dwelling stock, while adding nothing to housing demand,” Tapang said. “Policies that increase the cost or risk of investing in housing do not resolve that shortage but rather make it worse.” But the numbers also showed businesses are borrowing record amounts to construct apartment blocks and data centres. Building loans by businesses soared in value by 27.6 per cent in the quarter to be 51.8 per cent up over the past 12 months.

Advertisement

Loans for dwellings, predominantly units and apartment blocks, climbed 56 per cent over the year to a record $8.4 billion while loans for other buildings, including data centres, soared 84 per cent on an annual basis to more than $5 billion. The nation’s biggest home lender, the Commonwealth Bank, noted in its quarterly market update released on Wednesday that cost-of-living pressures and the impact of higher interest rates are starting to affect its borrowers. Bank CEO Matt Comyn said that while the economic growth was slowing, the overall economy remained resilient due to low unemployment and strong public and private infrastructure spending. “Higher inflation and interest rates continue to place uneven pressure on household incomes and business activity,” he said. title: Trump’s Fed nightmare: Rates won’t be slashed. They could surge now
text:

BusinessThe economyInflation Opinion Trump’s Fed nightmare: Rates won’t be slashed. They could surge now Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Updated November 11, 2026 — 3:34pm , first published 11:59am

Updated November 11, 2026 — 3:34pm ,first published 11:59am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. If Donald Trump expects Kevin Warsh, his hand-picked chair of the US Federal Reserve Board, to deliver the interest rate cuts that he has continuously clamoured for, he is about to be disappointed. Again. It now appears inevitable that the Fed will deliver its second rate rise in this cycle – the first was in September – after the US inflation rate came in above expectations for the third successive month. He won’t like it, but Donald Trump’s demands for lower interest rates will most likely be ignored by the Fed. Alex Brandon The only question – and just raising it will upset Trump – is whether the US central bank hikes its policy rate by 25 basis points or 50 basis points when it meets again next month. The US Bureau of Labor Statistics said on Tuesday that consumer prices rose 0.4 per cent in October. While calculations are muddied by the fact that a government shutdown meant there was no data collected in October last year, most calculations put the annual inflation rate at 4 per cent.

Advertisement

Even if energy and food costs are excluded to remove the direct effects of the war in the Middle East on oil and fuel costs, “core” inflation in October was 0.3 per cent and the annual core inflation rate 2.8 per cent – well above the Fed’s target of 2 per cent. Moreover, inflation is spreading across the US economy, thanks to Trump’s tariffs and the indirect effects of the higher oil and refined product prices on transport costs that are now feeding into goods and services prices. The only question – and just raising it will upset Trump – is whether the US central bank hikes its policy rate by 25 basis points or 50 basis points when it meets again next month. Fed officials are already preparing the ground for more than one rate hike. Fed governor Christopher Waller (a Trump appointee) told an audience in London on Tuesday that, should the inflation rate for the month come in above 0.3 per cent, a half-percentage point (50 basis point) rate rise might be needed. A conventional 25 basis point rise, he argued, would do little to win confidence that the Fed was serious about tackling inflation.

Advertisement

Advertisement

The inflation rate rose even though oil prices were mostly flat throughout the month. It would appear to be the delayed impacts of higher gasoline and, in particular diesel prices, that are now flowing through the economy and bleeding into consumer prices. The oil price has fallen back this month to trade at around $US92 a barrel and gasoline prices are sliding, albeit they are, at $US3.98 a gallon, still about 30 per cent higher than they were a year ago. Diesel prices are still 65 per cent higher than a year ago. Following the Democrats’ success in the midterms, Fed governors are less likely to feel intimidated by potential administration retaliations if they back rate rises. AP The oil price has been falling because oil flows from the Middle East have been restored to close to pre-war levels (albeit with far higher transport and insurance costs) and because Trump keeps saying that a negotiated end to the war is within reach, although he has said similar things throughout this year, but the conflict has yet to be resolved. With the US midterm elections out of the way, the administration may, however, find it easier to accede to some of Iran’s demands.

Advertisement

Even if the oil price continues to retreat, however, refined product prices – of which diesel is the key product – are unlikely to subside as quickly, as the wars in the Middle East and Ukraine have significantly damaged refinery capacity. The result of the midterms will help the Fed if it starts more aggressively raising US interest rates. That might infuriate the president, but there is little he can do about it. If the wars were to end soon, it would still take well into next year for volumes to recover. In the meantime, the higher cost of transporting goods and food will continue to push up goods and grocery prices. Tariffs remain another contributor to the inflation rate with their stop-start history, thanks to the courts consistently ruling them illegal and the Trump administration’s continuing efforts to reimpose them using new legislative headings. Toy prices, for instance, were 9 per cent higher than a year ago. Auto parts and repairs prices were up 0.6 per cent in October. Then there’s the impact of the boom in artificial intelligence, which is pushing up the prices of semiconductors and impacting the prices of computers, smartphones and other devices as well as electricity prices.

Advertisement

The inflation data underscores why US voters gave the Republicans such a thrashing at the midterm elections. For ordinary US households, the cost-of-living pressures are real and intensifying. Related Article Analysis

US midterms Donald Trump’s humiliation is an opportunity for America The result of the midterms – a Democrat majority in both chambers of Congress – will help the Fed if it, as expected, starts more aggressively raising US interest rates. That might infuriate a president who wanted Warsh to deliver greatly lower rates, but there is little he can do about it. Trump has tried, unsuccessfully, to remove former Fed chair Jerome Powell from the board, threatening to prosecute him for cost overruns in the renovations of the Fed’s Washington headquarters. He’s still trying to unseat another governor, Lisa Cook, with flimsy accusations of mortgage fraud. Even if he were able to sack Cook (there is a handpicked administration panel “investigating” her), or Powell decided to retire before his term ends in January 2028, the Democrats are most unlikely to approve a new Trump nomination to the board. And other Fed governors are now less likely to feel intimidated by potential administration responses to votes in favour of rate rises.

Advertisement

It’s not been a good week for Trump and his Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. On Monday, the Congressional Budget Office released its summary of the outcomes from the 2026 fiscal year which, in the US, ends on September 30. The Trump administration presided over a deficit of $US2 trillion ($2.9 trillion), or 6.2 per cent of GDP, a significant increase from the $US1.8 trillion (5.8 per cent of GDP) deficit in fiscal 2025. The administration is spending more (outlays were up 6 per cent) while, thanks to the One Big Beautiful Bill Act’s tax cuts for companies and the wealthy, generating only 3 per cent revenue growth. Corporate tax revenue fell 16 per cent. Customs revenue fell 11 per cent because the administration had to refund $US126 billion after the US Supreme Court deemed Trump’s original global tariffs illegal. Loading America’s finances aren’t improving. In October, the CBO estimates, there was a deficit of $US409 billion, 30 per cent more than the same month last year, with revenues shrinking and spending growing.

Advertisement

With government debt of more than $US40 trillion and the net interest cost of that debt climbing 11 per cent in the year to September, to $US1.14 trillion, a rising rate environment would only increase the threat to America’s financial stability and its ability to sustain even its modest – by comparison with other developed economies – social security net. Bessent, who promised to lower the deficit-to-GDP ratio to 3 per cent, says economic growth will fix America’s public finances. It won’t, and Trump’s second term will, just like his first term, leave a legacy of unfulfilled promises and unsustainable debt and deficits. Ordinary Americans will be much poorer for the experience. The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby Wallabies wary of Scotland’s Finn-and-Sione show Iain Payten November 11, 2026 — 3:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Edinburgh: One is among the world’s highest-paid rugby stars, armed with instinctive skills and the capacity to humiliate defences. The other is an Australian-raised Lion who didn’t get a crack at home and would love nothing more than leading Scotland to victory over the Wallabies. Together, the No.10-12 combination of Finn Russell and Sione Tuipulotu represents arguably the biggest threat to the Australian team when they return to Murrayfield on Monday morning (AEDT). And the Wallabies are aware. Loading “[Tuipulotu] and Finn Russell together, almost 150 caps together, there’s a great combination between those two,” Wallabies assistant coach John Ulugia said. “Both being in the British and Irish Lions shows that they’re class players. “He’s playing against Australia, so [Tuipulotu] is going to get motivated.”

Advertisement

The Wallabies take on the Scots in Edinburgh for the first time since 2024, when the Joe Schmidt side was flying after wins over England and Wales. But Tuipolotu turned in a superb performance as Scotland skipper against Australia, and led the hosts to a 27-13 win. On a heady day, he scored a try, won a points victory in a personal battle with Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii and was presented the Hopetoun Cup by his 77-year-old Scottish grandmother, Jaqueline Thomson, who had been flown over from Australia by a sponsor and was feted by the crowd. Sione Tuipulotu celebrates after scoring against the Wallabies in 2024. Getty Images Tuipulotu grew up in Melbourne and played for the Junior Wallabies and the Rebels, but having stalled at the franchise, he elected to move to Scotland. Via his heritage from his “Greenock granny”, Tuipulotu debuted for the Scots in 2021 and progressed to captain in 2024. “He’s class,” Wallabies halfback Ryan Lonergan said. “He’s super powerful and obviously a great leader for them. The way that he can square up their attack as well is something pretty special. We’ll look to shut him down.”

title: 'Can't put that in the cloud': Australians are turning to an old-fashioned safeguard
text:
The 27-tonne door to this vault has been under Sydney's centre for a century.

In October 1926, it took around 25 horses to move it from the wharf to its destination in Martin Place, where the rest of the building was constructed around it.

It's also one of the few still operated by a big bank.

Australian banks have reportedly closed hundreds of vaults alongside the closure of physical branches, with the costs of maintaining vaults becoming too expensive.

But as banks withdraw from the market, private operators are picking up their unwanted facilities.

ABC Bullion is among companies that manage private vaults. General manager Jordan Eliseo the company has found demand demand had at least "doubled, if not tripled in the last decade".

Volatility in financial markets and higher inflation tend to stimulate higher demand for gold and precious metals.

"We had the global financial crisis 20 years ago. You had the European debt crisis about 15 years ago. You had Brexit. You had the pandemic, and then you had last year," he told SBS News.

"All of those all of those events have seen gold demand, and therefore demand for things like private vaults increased quite quite substantially."

Common items stored in vaults include precious metals, family heirlooms and important documentation. Source: Supplied / Commonwealth Bank

Eliseo said there is strong demand in migrant communities, particularly those from China, India and Bangladesh.

"Consumers and households from those regions are typically quite friendly towards investing in gold. It's been a long trusted savings asset in those communities," he said.

There also tends to be higher usage of self-managed superannuation funds among these communities, according to Eliseo, where bullion can be used for retirement investment but may also require safe storage.

Westpac is the latest big bank to join ANZ and National Australia Bank in transitioning their vault services to private operators.

John Fleming, general manager at the Australian Security Industry Association, said it's a shift that allows banks to focus on their core services while private operators invest in vault offerings.

He said there has been "a lot of investment in these areas, and private people wouldn't invest in these areas if it wasn't a growth market".

As prices of precious metals like gold go up, Fleming said so does demand for ways to store them safely.

"People, even small homeowners who may have some jewellery at home who may not feel secure," he said.

"You can't put that in the cloud."

Items often stored in vault security include precious metals, diamonds, family heirlooms, hard drives and important legal documents.

Fleming said vault storage operators invest in thorough security measures.

"They put a lot of effort in, whether it's video surveillance, biometrics, on-site monitoring, or seismic detection through the wall, so that somebody from the outside trying to drill or make a hole in the wall gets picked up straight away," he said.

While other big banks move away from these services, Commonwealth Bank of Australia (CBA) said it's a growing area for them.

CBA operates 135,000 safe custody vaults and have added around 32,000 new vaults over the last two years. Monica Wegner, CBA's executive general manager of everyday banking, said CBA experiences more demand around cultural festivals.

"We do see amongst our vault customers that about half of the vaults are occupied by migrants to Australia," she said.

Commonwealth Bank of Australia branch in Martin Place, Sydney, contains one of the most opulent vaults in the country — with a door 700mm thick and weighing 27 tonnes. Source: AAP / Joel Carrett

"We observe people wanting to store things for different reasons," she said.

"Sometimes it's even natural disasters. You can imagine with things like fires, they don't want to have important documents at home. They want to have them in a safe space."

Wegner doesn't see demand shrinking any time soon.

"It's interesting because you might expect because other things are digitising, why would we still need these vaults?" she said.

"But at the end of the day, you still have customers that have things that are very precious to them."

title: Australia is in a $7 billion spending season. There's a warning before you buy
text:
In brief The ACCC has announced a sweep across retail sectors to investigate potential misconduct during the sales period.

It will be watching for misconduct such as inaccurate 'sitewide' or 'storewide' discount claims.

As shoppers look to score Black Friday and Cyber Monday deals this month, Australia's consumer watchdog is keeping a close eye on potentially misleading conduct through the sales period.

The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) has announced a sweep across multiple retail sectors, looking at potential misconduct, including: 'sitewide' or 'storewide' claims of discounts when products are excluded; inaccurate countdown timers; pressuring promotional tactics; and advertisements comparing sale prices to misleading reference prices.

Australians often spend close to $7 billion in the pre-Christmas shopping events, which fall on 27 and 30 November this year.

The watchdog says fine-print disclaimers for 'sitewide' or 'storewide' claims are not sufficient to qualify them, and when they're inaccurate, countdown timers can create a false sense of urgency.

It's the ACCC's third sweep of its kind, following similar investigations in 2024 and 2025 that led to penalties for companies that made false and misleading representations about their sales.

However, the ACCC says this is the first time the sweep will examine companies' practices across multiple channels, including websites, emails and social media.

It will also assess promotional practices over time and look for any improvements in compliance with consumer law in the past three years.

The ACCC has also encouraged consumers to focus on the final price of a product rather than promotional claims, check for any exclusions or conditions, and compare prices between retailers.

"Consumers should be able to trust that the advertised savings and discount prices are genuine, but we know some businesses use tactics to mislead consumers into thinking they are getting a bargain even when they are not," ACCC deputy chair Catriona Lowe said.

Black Friday scams

The ACCC also issued a warning about consumers buying products from illegitimate sellers and fake online shopfronts.

In the first nine months of 2026, 58.7 per cent of reports to the government's ScamWatch program that included financial loss were from buying and selling scams.

ScamWatch warned that scammers will impersonate legitimate businesses and familiar platforms to advertise fake products such as cars, second-hand clothing and concert tickets.

It also said artificial intelligence was making these scams "cheaper, faster and more convincing" with scammers using AI to generate product images, build websites and create compelling copy.

The ACCC's National Anti-Scam Centre has recorded over 20,000 successful takedowns of scam websites (many posing as online shopping sites) so far in 2026.

Last year, the ACCC also issued a warning about 'ghost stores', which falsely claimed they were local Australian businesses with closing-down sales and were instead based overseas and drop-shipping low-quality products to consumers.

However, ScamWatch notes that Australia has seen a slight decrease in the number of scam reports from January to September this year compared with the same period in 2025. Reported losses have also decreased by 3 per cent to just over $250 million.

title: 'Reaching people at every stage': Australia's retirement squeeze is worsening
text:
In brief The number of pre-retirees who feel prepared for retirement is now 28 per cent, compared to 38 per cent in 2025.

Three quarters of of retirees report inflation and cost of living were among the biggest influences on their financial position.

The number Australians who feel prepared for retirement has plunged in the past year and is now at its lowest level in a decade, according to a new report.

The number of pre-retirees who feel prepared for retirement is now 28 per cent, compared to 38 per cent in 2025, according to Brighter Super's annual Retirement Outlook Index.

Retirees living comfortably also fell from 58 per cent last year to 38 per cent in 2026, while confidence they have enough money to fund retirement fell from 60 per cent to 41 per cent.

The share of retirees covering just the basics or struggling more than doubled from 14 to 30 per cent.

A majority of both pre-retirees and retirees feel the cost of living is to blame, with three quarters of retirees reporting that inflation and cost of living were among the biggest influences on their financial position.

Julian Cappe, head of research at Investment Trends, said more pre-retirees are planning to cut spending in retirement to close the gap, rather than planning to save more.

"After 17 years of tracking how Australians approach retirement, this year's results show financial pressure reaching people at every stage, from those still working to those already retired," he said.

The report found people who sought financial advice were more likely to make extra contributions and to be less anxious about their prospects.

However, these factors could also correlate with higher incomes, underscoring unequal access to professional help.

READ MORE Which super funds earned a retirement tick of approval?

"Advice is expensive, so lower advice fees is certainly an area where many heading into retirement would be looking to their super fund to be able to provide them with," Cappe said.

The super needed for retirement

The amount that Australians need to retire comfortably is rising, according to figures released by the Association of Superannuation Funds of Australia (ASFA), the peak body for the super industry, in September.

A couple who own their home and are seeking a comfortable retirement will need $78,998 a year, or $1,513 a week. A single homeowner will need $56,166 a year, or $1,076 a week.

For homeowners aged 65 to 84, the budget for a comfortable retirement rose 0.5 per cent for couples and 0.4 per cent for singles in the June quarter.

ASFA CEO Mary Delanhunty said the rising cost of living is affecting retirees more due to the categories of goods they are spending their money on, including electricity, car costs, medical services, insurance and meals out.

"Retirees are among the groups hit hardest by the cost of living crisis because their budgets are weighted towards the things going up in price the most," Delahunty said.

Australian Taxation Office data shows the median super balance for those aged 60 to 64 is just over $200,000 — meaning retirees rely heavily on fund advice, tax strategies and government pension integration to stretch their savings.

title: David Walliams named after failed bid to block publication of grooming allegations
text:
In brief David Walliams was named as the celebrity who tried to stop misconduct allegations from being published.

A court rejected his bid to block reporting, clearing the way for the claims to be made public.

This article contains references to child abuse and suicide.

Two media groups named British comedian and bestselling children's author David Walliams on Tuesday as the high-profile figure who had tried to prevent allegations of sexual misconduct being published by saying he would take his own life if they were revealed.

The Guardian and ITV News said that Walliams, formerly a judge on music mogul Simon Cowell's "Britain's Got Talent" television show, had sought an injunction against the newspaper and the broadcaster ITN, which produces ITV News.

Walliams, who has sold more than 60 million books, had sought to block publication of the allegations, which he denies, primarily on the grounds that he would again attempt suicide if they were made public.

Reporting on the investigation on Tuesday, the Guardian said multiple women had accused Walliams of abusing his "power and position as a celebrity to prey on them for sexual purposes when they were teenagers or young women".

The Reuters news agency could not independently confirm the allegations, and a lawyer for Walliams did not reply to repeated requests from Reuters for comment.

Walliams wrote to investigating journalists

The Guardian said Walliams had written a personal letter to the investigating journalists, denying abusing his position of power.

"I realise that at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with ..." he wrote.

"And whilst a power imbalance is inevitable when one party is famous, abusing that power is something else entirely and it is something I never did.

"I am not a sexual predator."

The High Court in London rejected the application for an injunction on 3 November. It had been based on arguments about Walliams' right to life and right to freedom from inhuman or degrading treatment. The court did not name him, however.

Editors and media lawyers had said that granting the injunction for this reason would have set a worrying precedent for free speech. Similar injunction requests in the past have generally been based on individuals' privacy rights.

Once a 9 November deadline for Walliams to appeal had passed, the media groups were able to publish their investigation.

After being asked for a response in May ahead of publication of the allegations, Walliams expressed a desire to kill himself, and in July he attempted to do so, his lawyers told the High Court in October.

They said that Walliams denied the allegations, but that "shame arising from deep-rooted childhood trauma and the fear of 'trial by media'" if the investigation was published meant he was highly likely to take his own life.

The High Court said in a summary of its ruling that Walliams had a "serious and longstanding psychiatric vulnerability and an elevated underlying risk of suicide, independently of the proposed publications".

Judge Matthew Nicklin found in his ruling that publishing the allegations would in fact pose a risk to Walliams' life, but that suicide was not inevitable. He said the duty to protect Walliams had been assumed by the mental health services looking after him, not the court.

Bestselling author dropped by publisher

Walliams found fame on British television alongside creative partner Matt Lucas in the early 2000s with shows including the comedy sketch series Little Britain before launching a career as a children's author, with books such as The Boy in the Dress and Gangsta Granny.

He went on to appear on Britain's Got Talent but left in 2022 after remarks he made on the show were leaked, and he later apologised for "disrespectful comments" about contestants.

title: 'Massive overreaction': The uniquely Australian scandal that continues to unfold
text:
In brief Usman Khawaja says the entire Australian cricket team knew about ball tampering in 2018.

David Warner has backed Khawaja's claims, describing Cricket Australia's investigation as "rushed and botched".

Eight years after sandpapergate, explosive new claims by Usman Khawaja have reopened old wounds and raised fresh questions about who knew what during Australian cricket's biggest scandal.

Fresh accusations have been thrown this week, raising more questions about who was accountable and whether the sport's governing bodies did their due diligence.

A Cricket Australia investigation found Cameron Bancroft, Steve Smith and David Warner were involved in the ball-tampering incident during a Test match against South Africa in 2018. The trio were subsequently suspended and fined.

The scandal resurfaced this week after Khawaja, who retired from international cricket in January, claimed in his new autobiography, Sabr, that the entire team knew about the ball tampering and that it had also occurred in an earlier match.

The allegations contradict Cricket Australia's findings, as well other players who have always denied knowing about the tampering.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Mitchell Starc became the first current player to deny the allegations saying his recollection hadn't changed over time and him and his fellow bowlers knew nothing about the sandpaper use until it was caught out.

Warner has backed Khawaja, naming his claims as "100 per cent accurate" and labelled Cricket Australia's investigation as "rushed and botched".

Cricket Australia said it stood by its findings, with chief executive Todd Greenberg saying on Tuesday it would not reopen the investigation.

Khawaja has faced criticism over the timing of his allegations, which coincide with the release of his book.

Usman Khawaja made the claims in his autobiography, Sabr. Source: AAP / Robbie Goodall

However the claims have renewed debate about whether Australian cricket has fully confronted the fallout from the scandal.

Why sandpapergate shocked Australia

During Australia's third Test against South Africa in Cape Town in March 2018, Bancroft was caught using sandpaper to roughen one side of the ball to make it reverse swing and assist Australia's bowlers.

The public backlash was swift and widespread, with then prime minister Malcolm Turnbull describing the conduct as a "disgrace" and a "bitter blow to the pride of our country".

Cricket Australia banned Smith and Warner from playing for a year, with Bancroft banned for nine months. Warner was barred from ever being considered for a leadership position in Australian cricket. The trio was fined by the International Cricket Council, which also suspended Smith for one game.

Images of Smith breaking down in tears at a press conference made headlines around the world and the scandal prompted a wider reckoning within Australian cricketing culture.

Steve Smith broke down in tears when he faced a press conference following the scandal. Source: Getty / Steve Christo

Sport and controversy are rarely far apart, but Western Sydney University sociologist David Rowe says Australia's cultural connection to cricket made sandpapergate different.

"Cricket does have this … cultural status. It's kind of old school, gentlemanly," he told SBS News.

"Australia got caught, but it was a humiliation because it is traditionally the national game."

Rowe believes the public response was disproportionate to the offence, noting ball tampering was widespread and not unique to Australia. He pointed to a 1994 incident involving former England captain Michael Atherton who took dirt from his pocket and rubbed it onto the ball to alter its condition during a Test against South Africa. Atherton was fined £2,000 but retained the captaincy and avoided suspension.

"It was a massive overreaction [Australian public response] ... fuelled partly by a sense of shame," he said.

What has Khawaja claimed?

Cricket Australia's investigation found the incident was a one-off, and only Bancroft, Warner and Smith were involved.

But questions have persisted about other players' knowledge, with some believing the trio were used as scapegoats.

In 2021, Bancroft hinted bowlers knew about the sandpaper use, saying it was "pretty probably self-explanatory" given that altering the ball was meant to help the bowling attack.

That prompted current captain Pat Cummins and his fellow bowlers Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon to distance themselves from the scandal, saying in a statement they had no knowledge "of a foreign substance" being taken onto the field.

Current captain Pat Cummins has insisted he had no knowledge of the ball tampering. Credit: AAP

Khawaja has not explicitly alleged that those players knew sandpaper was being used but claimed the entire team was aware.

"It was all of us," Khawaja told Nine newspapers this week.

"Not the batters, not the bowlers, not the staff. All of us.

"I don't want to be the one who comes out and talks about the truth.

"The issue is that I genuinely thought after eight years the truth would have been out by now."

Khawaja said he spoke passionately in the change rooms after the 2018 match for the team to take collective responsibility, rather than blaming Warner, Smith and Bancroft.

"Obviously, it didn't work that way and those three guys got crucified," he said.

Cricket Australia has defended its investigation findings.

"There has been a great deal of speculation in the eight years since the 2018 Cape Town Test, including extensive media coverage throughout last month's series in South Africa," a spokesperson said in a statement at the weekend.

"During this time there has been the ongoing opportunity to present any relevant information and this remains the case.

"All relevant information presented to CA to date has been properly considered and we remain comfortable with the findings of our integrity process."

A scandal waiting to happen?

At the time of sandpapergate, Rowe noted the Australian team had developed a reputation for aggressive sledging and a win-at-all-costs mentality, making it unpopular among rival teams and their supporters.

An independent review commissioned after the scandal found Cricket Australia was "arrogant" and "controlling", with the team's culture partly to blame for the ball tampering.

"The ball-tampering incident at the Newlands Ground in South Africa can be seen as an aberration," it said.

"However, to think this would be mistaken. We have seen evidence that the structures built around elite cricket are oriented to winning, without properly counting the cost."

Since then, the team's image has arguably softened under the captaincy of Pat Cummins, who exhibits a calm and respectful leadership style.

Cummins last month distanced himself again from the scandal, saying it was a "long time ago".

"[I've] answered every question a million times so it was dealt with then ... all I can say is, as a group, we've moved on," he said.

What happens now?

On Tuesday, Cricket Australia chief executive Todd Greenberg all but ruled out reopening an inquiry.

"We don't see any compelling reason to open the investigation or revisit this again. I don't think there's anything that can be gained from that," he told SEN radio.

"We have said we're comfortable with the outcome of the investigation based on the information we've received.

READ MORE Johnny Mullagh: a cricketing icon recognised as a trailblazer

"That includes what we've seen from Usman, and our position hasn't changed on that."

Rowe believes that is a mistake.

"To essentially put up the drawbridge in the middle of this public controversy, I think is an an ill-advised approach to take," he said.

University of Sydney senior sports lecturer Dr Steve Georgakis said it would be difficult for the side to move on until there was full transparency about the allegations.

"Trust is an important thing, a connection that we have with these athletes is that they'll go out and do the right thing, and there's transparency and there's openness and there's no cover-ups," he told SBS News.

"Cricket Australia and the players need to tell us the truth, and from there we can move on."

title: Why Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's ties to Trump are back in the spotlight
text:
in brief Tech company Nvidia is investigating whether its CEO has been targeted by foreign intelligence.

Jensen Huang has close ties with Donald Trump.

US President Donald Trump’s close ties with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang have come under renewed scrutiny after revelations on Monday that the company’s board is investigating whether a foreign intelligence operation targeted the tech executive.

Huang, regarded as one of Trump’s closest allies in Silicon Valley, has cultivated a strong relationship with the president since at least 2025.

Nvidia's board launched its probe after a New York Times report said Huang had a close relationship with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, who US intelligence officials believe passed information to the Chinese government.

Nvidia shares closed more than 4 per cent lower on Monday.

"I’m pushing to investigate Jensen Huang and Nvidia to determine whether our national security was compromised," Democratic senator Chris Coons said in a post on X.

"We need answers about the relationship between AI billionaires and the Trump administration, who's making these decisions, and who's really got their hand on the wheel."

Democrats on the House of Representatives Foreign Affairs Committee wrote to US commerce secretary Howard Lutnick, calling on the Commerce Department to halt exports of advanced AI chips to China.

Gabe Amo, Gregory Meeks and Sydney Kamlager-Dove sought answers by 1 December on whether top officials at the Commerce Department were aware of US intelligence linking Alice Huang, a former executive of Singapore-based ⁠Megaspeed who is not related to the Nvidia CEO, to Chinese efforts to obtain Nvidia chips.

They also asked in their letter whether the top officials communicated with secretary of state Marco Rubio regarding Alice Huang and Megaspeed.

"If Commerce was not briefed, we need to know why. If it was briefed, we need to know how it responded. And if the Department knowingly permitted these exports despite credible national-security concerns, the American people deserve an explanation," the letter added.

Jensen Huang, the Nvidia CEO, has a direct line to the US president. A reporter from the Reuters news agency saw Huang's full name pop up on Trump's phone in December 2025.

Huang flew with Trump to China on the Air Force One presidential plane in May, the first visit by a US president to China in nearly a decade.

Huang attended a high-profile state dinner in September for Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House. The company committed US$25 million ($36.1 million) for Trump's planned White House ballroom, according to media reports.

The New York Times reported that Trump had been briefed on Huang's relationship with the woman and on intelligence that she was giving information to the Chinese government, and that he chose not to act on the information.

READ MORE Chinese AI app DeepSeek banned on all Australian government devices

The White House press office declined to comment further on Trump's relationship with Huang on Monday.

Trump doesn’t believe Alice Huang is a spy

Trump said on Monday the FBI was looking into the Nvidia CEO's affair with the Chinese businesswoman alleged to be a spy for Beijing. Trump said he had spoken to the CEO, who told him that he had no idea that the woman was a spy. Trump said he believed the CEO.

China's foreign ministry said the spy accusations were "groundless". Reuters could not determine Alice Huang's location to seek comment from her on Monday.

Huang's relationship with Trump has coincided with several favourable policy developments for the company.

In April 2025, the administration backed off plans to restrict exports of certain Nvidia AI chips to China after Huang attended a dinner at Trump's Mar-a-Lago club in Florida.

In December 2025, Trump said the US would allow Nvidia to export its H200 processors, its second-best AI chips, to China and collect a 25 per cent fee on such sales.

Trump has lavished Huang with praise, awarding him the nation's highest honour for scientific achievement in October.

The same day Trump gave Huang the award, the president disclosed buying up to US$1.6 million ($2.32 million) and selling up to US$1 million ($1.44 million) in Nvidia stock during the summer.

White House spokesperson Davis Ingle told Reuters at the time that third-party financial institutions independently manage the president's portfolio.

title: Anthony Albanese announces mandatory reporting after OpenAI's Medicare breach
text:
In brief Anthony Albanese said the government had accepted all recommendations of a rapid review into the breach.

The safeguards would include mandatory reporting of AI risks and the independent evaluation of frontier AI models.

Artificial intelligence companies will have to abide by new "mandatory" safeguards when operating in Australia, and a regulator will be established to enforce them, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has announced.

The measures would include "mandatory" reporting of AI security breaches and potential breaches of criminal law, as well as the independent evaluation of frontier AI models, Albanese told reporters on Tuesday.

The AI safety regulator will be tasked with implementing measures to keep the booming industry in check and will be able to impose penalties on AI companies that violate the rules.

The measures will form part of the federal government's upcoming AI safety regulation.

title: New Airbnb rules: What the changes mean for hosts and travellers
text:
IN BRIEF From 20 November, Airbnb is changing its rules to limit what hosts can ask guests to do before check-out.

Unexpected rules and requests after booking or during a stay have reportedly left some guests feeling misled.

Being faced with an endless list of chores when it's time to check out of your Airbnb stay isn't the best way to end a holiday.

Facing complaints from travellers, Airbnb is changing the rules to limit what hosts can ask guests to do before check-out. The new policy starts on 20 November.

What do the changes mean for hosts?

From November 20, hosts will need to re-check and revise their check-out chores to ensure they are simple and reasonable — and not "onerous".

For instance, they could ask guests to place used dishes in the sink rather than washing them, or gather towels in a designated place rather than launder them. This may help to avoid guest complaints and action from the platform.

The company suggests hosts should fully disclose their updated house rules and requests on the property page before guests get to the booking page.

Unexpected rules and requests after booking or during the stay can leave guests feeling misled, which can result in poorer stay experiences, bad reviews or complaints to the platform.

READ MORE The Bali venues taking a stand against bad tourist behaviour

The changes may also leave hosts with more cleaning to do. If so, hosts need to ensure they have adjusted their cleaning fee to reflect the actual cost.

However, they should also check whether their total price remains competitive compared to similar properties in the area.

What do the changes mean for travellers?

Travellers can expect a better check-out experience during their stay due to less time-consuming check-out chores.

However, while they are not required to perform work normally handled by a professional cleaner, they must still be responsible guests and leave the property in reasonable condition.

One practical tip for travellers is to always check the house rules and requests before booking.

They should keep a record, such as a screenshot or photograph, of any unexpected rules and requests introduced after the booking or during the stay. This can help if they need to report a problem to the platform.

Travellers should also be prepared for possible price increases. Some hosts may face higher cleaning costs if they can no longer rely on guests to complete certain tasks.

They may pass these additional costs on to travellers through higher cleaning fees or nightly rates.

Why have these changes been made?

Guests have questioned why they should pay a cleaning fee while still being expected to complete cleaning tasks themselves before checking out.

From their perspective, the problem is not simply how difficult each task is, but whether the overall exchange appears fair.

Guests may accept a cleaning fee when they believe it relieves them of the labour required to prepare the property for the next guest.

READ MORE The grim news for Australian travellers quietly updated this week

However, when the fee comes with a demanding list of chores, they may perceive the arrangement as less fair, as they may feel they are paying twice, once with money and again with their labour.

The new changes are therefore intended to create a fairer division of responsibilities and protect the guest experience on Airbnb.

Keeping both sides happy

Airbnb is a service platform whose value depends on both guests and hosts. This means Airbnb must consider whether the new changes are fair to both groups.

So far, the changes have sparked strong opposition from hosts.

They have called for a booking blackout on 20 November by closing their properties to new bookings, and started an online petition asking Airbnb to reconsider the rules.

The petition has attracted more than 27,000 signatures.

READ MORE Australians love traveling to the UK. They could soon be paying more

This response highlights the challenge Airbnb faces. A policy change that makes check-out easier for guests could leave hosts feeling neglected and with less control over their properties.

This may simply shift dissatisfaction from guests to hosts.

In response, some hosts may reduce their dependence on Airbnb by listing their properties on other platforms.

If enough disgruntled hosts switch completely to other platforms, it will risk the supply of properties on Airbnb and make the platform less attractive to guests.

What alternatives could Airbnb consider?

Rather than introducing policies that improve guest convenience at the expense of hosts, one possible way Airbnb could address this issue is to increase cost transparency to promote fairness to both guests and hosts.

For example, Airbnb could reintroduce a breakdown of cleaning fees in the pricing details. Hosts would need to explain how the fee is calculated and which cleaning services it covers.

This would help guests understand what they are paying for and what, if anything, they are still expected to do.

title: 'I thought I was going to die': The Australian story of 'harms' being told to the world
text:
In brief Australia is playing a key role at COP31 in Türkiye, with Climate Change Minister Chris Bowen acting as president of negotiations.

Ten Australians launched a case against the government in June, arguing it has a legal duty to protect people from climate harm.

Melissa Fisher says there was one night in her former home when the temperature crept past 35C, and she thought she was "going to die".

"I was so overheated. I started feeling very sick and drowsy and dizzy," she says.

"I started to panic that my brother would find me the next day and I would not be here because of how hot it was."

Fisher was living in a public housing unit in northern Adelaide at the time with no insulation, only concrete walls and a tin roof. She has since moved to another unit with temperature control.

She says there was "no sleeping" when heat lingered overnight in her last home and no relief because she couldn't take showers to cool off, due to a painful inflammatory skin condition.

Fisher is one of 10 claimants from across the country who launched a human rights case against the Australian government earlier this year, arguing it has a legal duty to protect people from climate harm.

The Hard Truths case

Known as the 'Hard Truths' case, the group, including First Nations people, firefighters and people living with disabilities, argue climate change is already causing them "devastating harm" and that the government's approval and subsidisation of coal and gas projects are fuelling escalating risks.

They outlined broad-ranging effects of climate change across the country, including floods, the Black Summer bushfires, the South Australian algal bloom and extreme heat.

According to their submission, by failing to regulate fossil fuel production in line with climate targets, the Australian government is violating the group's human rights, including the rights to life, privacy, family and home life, and culture.

Represented by the Human Rights Law Centre, Environmental Justice Australia and Earthjustice, they called on the United Nations Human Rights Committee to declare Australia's approval and subsidisation of coal and gas projects unlawful.

Mel Fisher (front left) said she is grateful claimants from the Hard Truth case could represent the group at COP31. Credit: Environmental Justice Australia

"We send so much coal overseas to be burnt and then the government wipes their hands of it and pretends it doesn't exist because we've sent it overseas. But the fact is the world doesn't have borders for gases and climate change," Fisher said.

According to Naru Research, led by climate and energy researcher Tim Baxter, emissions from Australia's exported fossil fuels "essentially doubled" between 2005 and 2020, while it has seen some decrease in emissions produced onshore.

Now, after launching the case in June, several members of the group are heading to this year's Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (COP31), which kicked off on Monday in Antalya, southern Türkiye.

They are attending to speak directly to the Australian government and participate in formal side events.

Fisher says she couldn't attend for medical reasons, but she's thankful some representatives of the case will attend the conference to raise awareness.

Australia at COP31

Australia is playing a key role as co-host at this year's COP, with Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen acting as the president of negotiations.

However, Australia's role is being scrutinised by experts and advocates, who argue there are conflicts between its domestic policy and what it's advocating for on the global stage.

Ahead of COP31, a letter signed by more than 500 academic experts from universities and research institutes, and addressed to Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, was published, outlining a "paradox at the heart of Australia's climate leadership".

The letter argued "Australia has pledged to represent its Pacific family on the world stage while advancing new and expanded coal and gas projects at home, with no plan to phase out production".

It also detailed what it called an "extraordinary convergence of events relevant to the climate crisis", including the glacier collapse in August that led to mass devastation and the deaths of more than 1,400 people in Nepal, and the announcement from the United Nations Environment Programme that 1.5C of global warming is now unavoidable.

Alina Leikin, principal lawyer from Environmental Justice Australia, told SBS News COP31 is presenting a "stark reality" for the Australian government.

"While Australia is playing this very important role, it hasn't really held up the mirror to its own policies — particularly when it comes to exports," she said.

Leikin said the claimants from the Hard Truth case are attending COP31 to relay "the catastrophic impacts of climate change" in their own lives to the global community.

Speaking to The Guardian's Australian Politics podcast last week about this criticism, Bowen said nations that export fossil fuels and those that import them are both managing energy transitions.

"Other ministers certainly recognise that Australia's doing well in its transition, that we've got great domestic decarbonisation plans in place," Bowen said.

In a statement to SBS News, the minister said COP31 is an "opportunity to show what cooperation can deliver at this crucial time for both our climate and global energy security".

"It will be about unlocking finance and investment, cheaper energy for households, accelerating electrification and boosting action on the ocean, nature's greatest climate regulator," he said.

A 'landmark' ruling sets out a path

The Hard Truths case is the first case to be filed in an international court or body against a country for climate harm since a landmark ruling by the International Court of Justice (ICJ) last year that paved the way for such action.

The advisory opinion delivered in July 2025 laid out obligations for states related to climate change, citing international treaties including the Paris Agreement (which set the goal of limiting global warming to 1.5C above pre-industrial levels) and international law, including human rights law and environmental law, including the duty to prevent significant harm to the environment.

While non-binding, the ruling clarified that even though the climate crisis has been caused by many countries and entities, the failure of states to take action to protect the climate system from greenhouse gas emissions may be an "internationally wrongful act which is attributable to that state".

Rebekkah Markey-Towler, a research fellow from Melbourne Climate Futures at the University of Melbourne, told SBS News it had broad implications for climate litigation around the world.

READ MORE Meet the young people who could outlive their own country

"It was a significant and a landmark moment in that regard to say to countries 'You have a responsibility to act on climate change and if you don't, there are going to be consequences under international law,'" she said.

Markey-Towler said the launch of a case against the Australian government was not surprising after the ICJ ruling, and Australia has been a "hotspot for climate litigation" for several decades.

Fisher says being involved in the Hard Truths case has felt "meaningful" and she takes pride in "putting pressure on the government to do more for climate change".

For now, the group is awaiting the government's response to their challenge. Fisher says she hopes they could see a pause on coal and gas activity until they get a result.

title: Australia's weapon against inflation has a side effect. Is there an alternative?
text:
IN BRIEF Some politicians are calling for alternatives to interest rates be considered to tackle inflation.

Economists say rate controls are the most effective tool.

Australia's cash rate is now at the highest it's been since the global financial crisis in late 2008 and many are feeling the pain.

With growing anxiety about the economy, whether the war in Iran will continue to drive up inflation, and the soaring cost of living, some Australians are wondering whether there are other ways to curb inflation than the "blunt instrument" of interest rate hikes.

The push for alternatives is also being fuelled by federal politicians including Greens leader David Shoebridge and independent senator David Pocock, who's calling for a "rethink on how we tackle inflation".

Pocock is pushing for a Senate inquiry to explore alternatives.

The campaign to steer away from rate rises

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Australia has used interest rates to manage inflation since the 1990s, with the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) aiming to keep it between 2 and 3 per cent. Lifting rates is intended to reduce house prices and household spending, and affects the exchange rate by reducing domestic spending.

But some say it's not effective in the current environment.

The left-leaning Australia Institute think tank says the main driver of inflation today is soaring fuel prices prompted by the war in Iran and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz — something which the RBA has no control over.

"It doesn't matter whether they put them up as they did to 4.85 per cent, they put them up to 5 per cent, they put them up to 10 per cent, they put them up to 20 per cent — that is going to do nothing to open the Strait of Hormuz," Australia Institute senior economist Matt Grudnoff said in a recent podcast.

"They're not connected in any way."

He also pointed to the inflationary impact of the growth of AI data centres, something the RBA has acknowledged. Demand for workers, material and land, as well as water and electricity, is coming at a time when the economy is operating at close to capacity.

"These two big forces that are pushing inflation, Australian interest rates will do nothing to impact them," Grudnoff said.

Pocock has put forward terms of reference for a Senate inquiry to look into alternatives to rate hikes. It hasn't yet been agreed to by parliament.

"There has to be a better way, and I've had so many Canberrans and people across the country writing and saying, 'hang on, this is madness, we have to find a better way to find a few more levers to pull and control inflation'," he told ABC News last week.

Greens leader David Shoebridge is also pushing for alternatives, saying: "It's time for a different approach, one that actually takes into account the real drivers of inflation: AI data centres, illegal wars and the 1 per cent."

What are the alternatives to rate hikes?

There are a number of levers available, including targeted tax increases, cutting government spending or lifting compulsory super contributions.

Raising the GST would be another option to stem consumption, but experts say it won't be as effective because it doesn't impact asset prices or the exchange rate. Then there's the hurdle of getting it cleared by various levels of state and federal parliaments, and regulatory monitoring to ensure businesses aren't profiteering.

"It sounds nice in theory, but it would probably be very impractical to put into play in reality," macroeconomist Luke Hartigan from the University of Sydney told SBS News.

Another option is the super guarantee — by lifting compulsory contributions.

"What it means is that people will put more money into their savings account ... if we wanted to take some heat out of the economy," Hartigan said.

"Again, it only affects the one channel of monetary policy, that cash rate, the cash flow channel; it won't affect the exchange rate."

He also said this alternative may not be fair on younger people who are more likely renting.

"The other thing is we don't know what will happen or how much we need people's incomes to go up or down," Hartigan said.

Another option is targeted tax increases on certain populations — for example, older homeowners who may be shielded from rate hikes. That too, Hartigan says, would only affect cash flow rather than exchange rate or asset prices.

And it's also politically difficult and would need the government to make an unpopular decision.

The political parties also have ideas. The Liberal Party argues curbing government spending would tackle inflation.

Diana Mousina, deputy chief economist at AMP, says cutting government spending would also come at a cost.

She said returning government spending to the historical average of around 23 per cent of GDP, compared to the current 28 per cent, would need around $135 billion in spending cuts.

"That would be an enormous fiscal adjustment," she wrote in a recent briefing paper.

"Cutting spending can mean fewer government services, lower payments or reduced programs, while higher taxes leave households with less disposable income.

"The pressure may fall on different parts of the economy than it does with higher interest rates, but somebody still has to spend less."

Meanwhile, Shoebridge has proposed national rent controls, halting the construction of new data centres and hiking company taxes.

Treasures Jim Chalmers has framed the government's changes to negative gearing, capital gains taxes and trusts as moves against financial inequality, whilst also acknowledging Australian households are hurting.

'No painless way out'

Mousina says there is no simple policy that allows us to bring inflation down without some economic cost.

"If inflation reflects demand running ahead of the economy's capacity to supply goods and services, ultimately demand needs to slow or supply needs to increase."

Hartigan says interest rates remain the most effective way of managing inflation.

"We don't like them, but they're better than the alternative, unfortunately," Hartigan said.

"We need to take some medicine. It's going to be bad medicine, so there's no easy way out of fixing inflation.

"There's no painless way out, unfortunately."

title: Manosphere content could get shut down, inquiry hears, amid minister's denial
text:
IN BRIEF A Senate inquiry is hearing submissions into the the government's digital duty of care bill.

Wayne Holdsworth, whose son Mac died after a sextortion scam, urged politicians not to turn online safety into a political contest.

This story contains references to suicide

New laws aiming to reform online platforms so they don't cause harm to children could "shut down the manosphere", drown businesses in red tape, and stifle free speech, an inquiry has heard.

Bereaved parents told a Senate inquiry into the government's digital duty of care bill that safer platform design and enforcement are urgently needed, but Liberal senator Sarah Henderson and tech company executives argued that new categories of harm are too broad and the bill is poorly written.

The Digital Duty of Care Bill aims to force online services, including social media platforms, search engines, apps, games, and AI chatbots, to ensure Australians enjoy a safe digital environment.

Users may be given a choice between algorithm-recommended content and a feed limited to people and pages they follow. Companies that fail to comply with the new rules could face fines of up to $109 million.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Communications Minister Anika Wells said the volume of image-based abuse reports to eSafety shows Australians are not adequately protected.

"If you build it, you are responsible for its risks," Wells told Nine's Today program on Monday, arguing the bill would establish basic safety standards and require companies to address risks in their products.

Where safety meets speech

Henderson said vague references such as "hostile attitudes towards women" could limit legitimate debate, saying Wells told her the bill was not about stopping the manosphere, but a departmental briefing suggested otherwise.

"It seems this is more about shutting down free speech than tackling harm," Henderson said. "Now the mandatory codes and standards are being removed and replaced with guidelines [made by the eSafety commissioner] that are not enforceable".

Wells previously told the National Press Club Australians could still listen to manosphere podcasts, arguing the bill wouldn't lead to government censorship.

Vague, undefined categories of material "harmful to children" or that "encourages or promotes hostile attitudes towards women or gender equality" or "encourages dangerous stunts" are problematic, tech companies and Henderson said.

TikTok's Jessika Lofstedt said the bill replaced "certainty with ambiguity and with subjectivity". She warned that platforms might over-moderate contentious material to avoid penalties.

Google and Meta also called for clearer definitions, including which recommender systems are being regulated and what new powers the eSafety Commissioner may create.

Romy Listo from Our Watch, which works to prevent violence against women, told the inquiry the bill was not about stopping people from expressing views but requiring platforms to manage risks linked to gendered drivers of violence, including content that condones violence against women or promotes rigid gender stereotypes.

"Some of the messages in the manosphere are harmful and research points to misogyny and violence towards women attitudes coming from there," Listo said.

The Free Speech Union's Ruben Kirkham, a computer scientist, questioned whether platforms could realistically monitor billions of posts each day, warning the resources required may exceed available computing capacity. He estimated the cost to run an AI detection tool across Australian content would consume 2 per cent of Australia's energy.

"The resource load to police the three billion pieces of social media content made every day … there may not actually be data centres and services sufficient to implement this," he said.

Heads Up Alliance founder Dany Elachi, founder of Heads Up Alliance, which calls for delayed use of smartphones and social media by children, said the bill was ideologically driven and warned it could be "weaponised".

"[The bill contains] manufactured input from left-leaning organisations funded by the government to lobby the government back on issues the government wants to be lobbied on," Elachi said.

Henderson questioned the Australian Computer Society (ACS) about why a café or a plumber should be subject to new obligations under the duty of care to conduct risk assessments of their online activity. ACS said it will help businesses with risk assessments.

"This level of bureaucracy for small businesses is completely unjustified," Henderson said.

Families suffer consequences of online abuse

Mia Bannister, founder of Ollie's Echo, told senators her 14-year-old son Ollie had experienced online abuse and anorexia before his death by suicide. She said harm could not always be reduced to "one post and one message".

“Ollie was a boy with anorexia," she said. "Gendered assumptions can leave boys unseen, their symptoms unrecognised and their distress dismissed."

Mia Bannister's son Ollie died by suicide after he was bullied online.

Emma Mason said her daughter Tilly experienced online bullying before her death by suicide at 15 in 2022. In one incident, a fake nude image of Tilly was shared with almost 3,000 people within hours, Mason said.

She told the inquiry that police had cited a lack of jurisdiction over Snapchat, an international company operating in Australia.

"We cannot keep asking children and families to carry the consequences of the risks that could and should have been identified earlier," Mason said. "Safety by design is mandatory in every part of the commercial world except in the digital world."

Wayne Holdsworth, whose son Mac died after a sextortion scam, urged politicians not to turn online safety into a political contest.

He said he had spoken to more than 300 groups since his son's death, adding: "We need to act now."

Platforms questioned over self-harm content

Independent senator David Pocock challenged TikTok over self-harm material on the platform, asking why content that breached its rules remained available and attracted thousands of likes.

"You big platforms turn up and absolve yourselves of responsibility," Pocock said. "Why do you allow self-harm content on your platform?"

Why, he asked, was a post with almost half a million likes trending if it went against the platform's guidelines?

TikTok representative Lofstedt said self-harm content was prohibited, but "we don't get it right every time" and offered to look at specific cases while rejecting the suggestion TikTok has a widespread problem.
